Summary
- The European Commission accepted Temu's action plan on October 26, 2026.
- The plan aims to remedy a breach of the Digital Services Act by Temu.
- This decision was announced from Brussels.
- The acceptance signifies a formal step in DSA enforcement.
What Happened
For compliance officers and legal teams at other Very Large Online Platforms, Temu's accepted plan could serve as an important benchmark.
The European Commission announced on October 26, 2026, from Brussels, its formal acceptance of an action plan submitted by the e-commerce giant, Temu. This crucial development signifies a step forward in addressing a previously identified violation of the Digital Services Act (DSA) by the online platform. The plan outlines specific measures Temu intends to implement to rectify the breach and ensure full adherence to the stringent regulations set forth by the EU.
The Commission's endorsement of Temu's action plan is a direct response to the platform's non-compliance with certain provisions of the DSA. This acceptance indicates that the proposed remedies are deemed sufficient by the regulatory body to bring Temu into line with its obligations under the landmark European legislation. This marks a significant moment in the ongoing efforts to enforce digital service regulations across the European Union.
Legal Context
The Digital Services Act (DSA) represents a cornerstone of the European Union's regulatory framework for online platforms, particularly those designated as Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) due to their substantial user base. Enacted to foster a safer, more transparent, and accountable online environment, the DSA imposes a wide array of obligations on these platforms, ranging from robust content moderation policies to enhanced transparency around advertising and recommender systems. The legislation aims to protect users from illegal content, disinformation, and manipulative practices, while also safeguarding fundamental rights.
When a platform is found to be in breach of the DSA, as was the case with Temu, the European Commission has the authority to demand corrective actions. The submission and subsequent acceptance of an action plan, such as the one from Temu, is a standard procedure in the enforcement process, allowing platforms to detail their strategy for achieving DSA compliance. This mechanism underscores the Commission's commitment to ensuring that digital service providers operating within the EU market uphold the high standards mandated by the Act, thereby reinforcing the integrity of online spaces for European citizens.
Why It Matters
The European Commission's acceptance of Temu's Digital Services Act action plan carries considerable weight for the broader landscape of online platform regulation and enforcement within the EU. This decision not only highlights the Commission's resolve in actively enforcing the DSA but also provides a tangible example of the expected remediation process for platforms found in violation. For compliance officers and legal teams at other Very Large Online Platforms, Temu's accepted plan could serve as an important benchmark. It offers insights into the specific types of measures and commitments the Commission deems appropriate for addressing DSA breaches, thereby informing their own strategies for proactive compliance and potential future remediation efforts.
Furthermore, this development reinforces the message that the EU is serious about holding major digital players accountable for their operations. The proactive engagement of the European Commission with platforms like Temu demonstrates a clear path for Digital Services Act enforcement EU-wide, emphasizing that online platform regulation action plan submissions are a critical component of addressing non-compliance. This ongoing regulatory scrutiny is vital for maintaining user trust and ensuring a fair and safe digital marketplace across the continent, setting a precedent for how future DSA breach remedy situations might be handled.
Practical Implications
Compliance officers for Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) should analyze the specifics of Temu's accepted action plan as a benchmark for developing their own DSA compliance strategies and preparing for potential enforcement actions, understanding the Commission's expectations for remediation.

The prime minister identified funding the government’s defense investment plan and establishing a route toward NATO’s spending targets as key priorities. He also stressed that national security must remain central to government policy in what he described as a “challenging world.”

articles.title: France's debt woes in focus as ECB meets | Gulf Times - Gulf Times
articles.summary: France's debt woes in focus as ECB meets | Gulf Times  Gulf Times
articles.full_text:
France's deteriorating public finances will take centre stage when the European Central Bank (ECB) meets this week, but policymakers are not expected to throw a lifeline to the eurozone's second-biggest economy just yet.
The ECB is set to keep interest rates on hold, having already hiked them twice this year, walking a fine line between tamping down inflation fuelled by the Iran war energy shock and supporting the eurozone economy.
But the focus of Thursday's meeting is likely to shift quickly to France and "how the ECB will respond to the ongoing fiscal and political crisis," said Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics.
French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, surged to their highest level since 2002 last week amid a standoff over next year's budget, which aims to reduce the country's vast debts.
Concerns have also been fuelled after protests, driven in part by demands for more spending on public services, degenerated into the worst street violence in years.
There has been speculation that the ECB could, for the first time, use a crisis-fighting tool aimed at combatting sharp movements in markets to push down French bond yields.
However, the criteria to activate the so-called Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) are strict, and most observers believe France's problems do not meet the threshold.
The ECB stipulates that the tool can only be used to counter "unwarranted" moves in markets, where there is a risk of financial stress spreading -- but not in cases where problems stem from poor fiscal policy.
So far ECB President Christine Lagarde, who also once served as France's finance minister, has sounded cool about the idea.
Asked about France's rising yields earlier this month, she responded: "The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies."
France's central bank chief, who sits on the ECB's governing council, also downplayed the prospect of an intervention, saying that "conditions are not met" for the central bank to step in.
Kenningham of Capital Economics predicted there would be "no lifeline for France" at Thursday's meeting, saying spreads between French and German bonds, the eurozone benchmark, would need to widen far more to justify any action.
Despite rising inflation caused by higher energy prices, the central bank for the 21 nations that use the euro is expected to keep its benchmark rate steady at 2.5%.
The ECB's rate call will come a day after the Federal Reserve announces its latest decision, with the US central bank also expected to stay on hold following a hike in September.
Eurozone inflation rose to a three-year high of 3.8% in September, although closely watched core inflation -- excluding volatile energy and food prices -- hardly changed.
There have so far been "very little knock-on effects from higher energy prices," ING economist Carsten Brzeski told AFP.
And France's crisis had "actually lowered chances of another rate hike," he said, adding that the "bond markets have taken over the ECB's task".
Rising bond yields cause tighter financing conditions and can push up borrowing costs for businesses and households, similar to the impact of higher rates.
Most economists predict the ECB will make the final hike of its current tightening cycle in December when it will be armed with updated growth and inflation forecasts.
Lagarde is also likely to face questions about her future as speculation intensifies she will step down before her term as ECB chief officially ends in October next year.
She has been linked to the top job at the World Economic Forum, which hosts a gathering of the global elite every year in the Swiss Alps resort of Davos.
But she has been tight-lipped so far, saying at the ECB's last meeting in September there was "nothing to report" on the matter.

articles.title: First Harmonised Technical Standard Published Under the EU AI Act - Orrick
articles.summary: First Harmonised Technical Standard Published Under the EU AI Act  Orrick
articles.full_text:
5 minute read        | October.27.2026    
On 14 October 2026, the European Commission published the first harmonised standard under the EU AI Act: EN 18286:2026 – Artificial intelligence – Quality management system (Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274). Compliance with this standard can be relied upon by providers of high-risk AI systems to demonstrate compliance with Articles 11(1) (Technical Documentation) and 17(1) (Quality Management System) of the AI Act.
We explain the role of harmonised standards under the AI Act and provide an overview of EN 18286.
The AI Act follows the EU New Legislative Framework (NLF) approach to product regulation. 1 Legislation establishes essential requirements for products, while harmonised European standards provide the technical details that support compliance with them. Some address the technical conformity of products, others organisational processes such as quality management.
Under the AI Act, essential requirements for high-risk AI systems are set out in Chapter III, Section 2 (Articles 8-15) of the Act. Providers must ensure that their high-risk AI systems comply with these requirements before their systems are placed on the market in the EU.
EN 18286 was jointly prepared by the European Committee for Standardisation (CEN), and the European Committee for Electrotechnical Standardisation (CENELEC), in response to a formal request from the European Commission to prepare standards covering 10 strategic areas: risk management, governance and quality of datasets, recordkeeping, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity, quality management and conformity assessment.
Once a standard’s reference is published in the Official Journal of the European Union (OJ), Article 40 of the AI Act provides a presumption of conformity with the requirements covered by that standard. Applying harmonised standards, in whole or in part, is voluntary and providers are free to demonstrate compliance with essential requirements in other ways.
Importantly, as pointed out in the 2022 Blue Guide on the implementation of the product rules, harmonised standards do not replace the binding essential requirements set out in the law. A technical specification in a standard presents an option for complying with the legal obligation. In risk-related harmonisation legislation, such as the AI Act, this means providers remain responsible for assessing all the risks of their AI system in order to determine which essential (or other) requirements are relevant.
A provider that relies on harmonised standards to demonstrate compliance with its obligations under the AI Act benefits from a presumption of conformity, but only in relation to the legal requirements covered by those standards
EN 18286 requires providers to identify the requirements under the AI Act that apply to them, define the scope of their quality management system and adopt a documented strategy for regulatory compliance. That strategy covers the essential requirements of Articles 9 to 15 of the AI Act, conformity assessment, modifications, post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting.
The standard then builds these into management-system processes covering leadership, roles and accountability, competence and resources, throughout the AI system lifecycle (including design and development, verification and validation, data management, continuous learning systems and retirement), supply chain controls, handling of non-compliance and management review.
The standard is designed to sit within an organisation's wider AI governance framework: it follows the same high-level management-system structure as ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management systems) and ISO 9001, so its regulatory-compliance processes can be integrated into an existing AI management system, or into a sector-specific quality management system.
According to the European Commission, EN 18286 is “designed to be layered on top of the existing international standards – such as ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 9001 or a sectoral QMS (e.g. ISO 13485) – rather than replace them.”
Adherence to these other standards on their own, however, will not allow a provider to benefit from the presumption of conformity.
For most high-risk AI systems, applying harmonised standards such as EN 18286 does not change the conformity assessment route. Harmonised standards affect the route only for biometric systems under Annex III, point 1, where providers may opt for self-assessment if harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied to all the essential requirements.
Otherwise, assessment by a notified body is mandatory. AI systems covered by points 2 to 8 of Annex III must be self-assessed by providers, whether or not they rely on harmonised standards.
The Official Journal publishes the reference, not the full standard. The standard is generally distributed for purchase by national standardisation bodies, including AFNOR (France), DIN (Germany), UNI (Italy) and BSI (UK). Buying it provides access to technical specifications, not certification or proof of compliance. Prices vary from one organisation to the next.
The paid-access model for harmonised standards is controversial and legally contested, given the importance of standards to legal compliance and their status as part of EU law.
EN 18286 is the first OJ-cited standard in a wider European AI standardisation programme. Commission standardisation request C(2025) 3871 final identifies 10 standardisation areas: risk management, data governance and quality, recordkeeping and logging, transparency and information to users, human oversight, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity, quality management (including post-market monitoring), and conformity assessment.
These areas relate principally to Articles 9–15, 17 and 43 of the AI Act. Ten areas do not necessarily mean 10 individual standards: several deliverables may address a single area. The remaining standards are at different stages of development and adoption.
Providers of high-risk AI systems should assess their compliance arrangements against EN 18286 to benefit from the presumption of conformity under Article 40. Existing ISO/IEC 42001 or ISO 9001 processes may be relevant but should not be assumed to satisfy Article 17. Providers should monitor the remaining harmonised standards as they are published.
1 The central instruments relating to harmonised standards are Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 (accreditation and market surveillance), Decision No 768/2008/EC (common framework for marketing products and conformity assessment) and Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 (European standardisation).

articles.title: How the EU AI Act Regulates Agentic AI - HackerNoon
articles.summary: How the EU AI Act Regulates Agentic AI  HackerNoon
articles.full_text:
We know that technology moves much faster than regulation. By the time a regulation has been drafted, debated, approved, and has entered into force, months have gone by and the technology has already advanced in ways that may require substantial regulatory changes.
Nothing provides a better example than the regulation of AI Agents under the EU AI Act. Exactly how and where Agentic AI fits within the wider EU Regulation may cause companies headaches and require clearer guidance from the EU down the line.
 
What the EU says
Currently, the main piece of official guidance from the EU is set out in a FAQ on the EU AI Act.
First, the EU clarifies that, whilst not explicitly mentioned in the Regulation, AI Agents qualifies as an AI system as per Art. 3(1), because they typically contain a general-purpose AI (GPAI) model and “have some form of interface” (which may be considered a system component). The FAQ acknowledges that
a more precise statement than ‘typically’ is difficult to make as the term AI agent is not legally defined and is used colloquially for different kinds of artefacts.
 
In light of this, rules applicable to AI systems can therefore also apply to agentic AI, including:
- any prohibited use (Art. 5)
- transparency requirements (Art. 50)
- GPAI requirements (Chapter V)
- obligations for high-risk AI systems and components applicable from 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028, respectively (Chapter III)
The FAQ further recognises that these considerations remain preliminary, and the AI Office will consider issuing more targeted strategies to address Agentic AI risks.
 
The “AI Agents Under EU Law” regulatory architecture
In a nutshell, the EU guidance tells you that if you develop or deploy Agentic AI, you must treat it as any other AI system. But at present, it remains rather brief, cursory at best.
Luckily, EU policy expert Luca Nannini and eight co-authors published in April 2026 a paper titled AI Agents Under EU Law: A Compliance Architecture for AI Providers, outlining a comprehensive framework for Agentic AI compliance with the EU AI Act.
Echoing the EU’s official guidance, the paper restates that AI Agents are not a separate legal category under the AI Act. Rather, they are assessed under the same framework as other AI systems, despite the fact that their distinctive features (autonomy, tool use, delegation, adaptation) will arguably make existing requirements harder to implement. The paper aims to clarify how to translate these requirements into practical engineering and governance measures.
 
Taxonomy
Firstly, the paper proposes a taxonomy of nine categories of Agentic AI use, spanning customer service, recruitment, coding, finance, marketing, research, IT operations, healthcare and personal assistants. The distinction in use case is highly consequential in terms of regulatory obligations: a recruitment assistant may trigger high-risk requirements, while a research agent may primarily raise transparency, privacy and copyright questions.
 
Compliance challenges
The greater regulatory compliance efforts demanded by Agentic AI stems from the distinctive risks - and related obligations under the AI regulations – posed by Agents. In particular, the authors emphasise:
- Cybersecurity. Tellin an Agent what it may or may not do is not a sufficient or viable security measure. Permissions must be enforced through external controls, comprising restricted credentials, API authorisation and limits on accessible tools.
- Human Oversight. As the latest Agentic AI incidents illustrated, Agents may bypass monitoring, inaccurately report results or behave unexpectedly. Hence, independent technical controls become even more important to ensure effective human oversight.
- Transparency. Because of the autonomy granted to them, Agents can affect people beyond the direct user (e.g., email recipients, customers, individuals whose records are changed). As such, transparency design must account for these wider interactions and preserve traceability.
- Runtime Behavioural Drift. The paper distinguishes: a) anticipated adaptation (behaviour already tested, documented and assessed); b) post-deployment learning (changes that may require reassessment if unanticipated); c) emergent drift (unexpected changes arising from memory, novel tool combinations or evolving strategies). Authors argue that compliance cannot be demonstrated where behavioural changes cannot be detected and characterised.
 
The wider EU regulatory environment
The EU digital regulation environment is anything but siloed: multiple EU regulations will apply to your AI system(s), beyond the EU AI Act. Ensuring compliance with the AI Act will not be enough, and you’ll need to comply with the wider EU regulatory ecosystem, comprising:
- General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It may apply whenever personal data is used to train AI agents, or agents process it to achieve the objective.
  - Example : a customer service agent receiving personal data in query, querying a CRM system, logging conversations, or sending confirmation emails may trigger GDPR’s Art. 6 (Lawfulness of Processing).
- Data Act. It governs the access to, sharing of, and portability of data generated by connected IoT devices and their “related services.”
  - Example : smart home agents monitoring IoT sensors, compiling an energy usage report, or recommending improvements will need to respect users’ data-access rights and applicable requirements to share data with third parties at users’ request.
- Digital Services Act (DSA). It regulates online intermediaries, hosting services, and online platforms, mandating content moderation transparency and accountability.
  - Example : content moderation agents flagging posts, reducing their visibility in a feed and sending notifications, as well as marketing agent publishing AI-generated reviews must meet applicable requirements concerning statements of reasons, transparency and risk assessments.
- Cyber Resilience Act (CRA). It prescribes mandatory, lifecycle cybersecurity requirements for “products with digital elements” (hardware and standalone software placed on the EU market with network connectivity)
  - Example : coding agents sold as standalone software with network connection need to be applicable secure-by-design, Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), vulnerability-reporting (from September 2026), and conformity (by October 2027) requirements.
- Revised Product Liability Directive (PLD). Taking effect in late 2026, the revised PLD will expand strict liability to digital products, holding economic operators liable for damage caused by defective AI systems.
  - Example : a financial advisory agent recommending selling based on outdated data (RAG caching bug) and causing significant loss to a client may expose its provider to liability; where Article 15 applies, non-compliance may also be relevant evidence of a defect.
- NIS2 Directive. It imposes strict cyber risk-management obligations on critical infrastructure sectors (e.g., energy, transport, healthcare).
  - Example : IT operations agents deployed by an energy utility to monitor SCADA or autonomously remediating via OT API access must report any incident within 24 hours, guarantee supply chain security and demonstrate that appropriate cybersecurity risk management measures are in place.
- Data Governance Act. It regulates “data intermediation services” and promotes voluntary data sharing across the EU.
  - Example : an agentic platform operating a data marketplace on which users contribute interaction data for training other agents must comply with notification, structural separation and neutrality obligations.
The paper argues that conformity with CRA directly support the corresponding AI Act cybersecurity assessment, where the statutory conditions are satisfied. Simultaneously, it acknowledges that conventional product-security standards may not fully address agent-specific threats.
 
Agentic AI compliance in practice
Given these considerations and regulatory interdependencies, the ideal compliance journey for Agentic AI developers and deployers may entail the following steps:
- Scope the system: establish what constitutes the regulated system, including sub-agents. Depending on their functions and how they are supplied, sub-agents may require separate conformity assessments or be subjected to different regulatory requirements.
- Map the GPAI layer: identify model providers, determine who bears GAPI obligations and obtain relevant documentation.
- Classify the system: document its intended purpose, implement contractual and technical restrictions where developers cannot predict how deployers will use the platform, and define risk classification.
- Establish a quality management system (QMS): identify applicable lifecycle requirements, including post-deployment behavioural monitoring, or integrate requirements sector-specific QMSs where they already exist (ISO 13485 for medical devices, IATF 16949 for automotive).
- Establish risk management: assess safety, fundamental rights and autonomy risks.
- Implement data governance: manage datasets, operational feedback and bias.
- Design for trustworthiness: implement oversight, transparency and traceability with a focus on automation boundary (which action the agent can execute autonomously and which require human oversight).
- Implement AI-specific cybersecurity: enforce permissions outside the model and build “non-human identity governance infrastructure” (comprising just-in-time credential provisioning, per-action authorisation, and credential rotation policies that account for the agent’s autonomous operation cycle).
- Assess CRA applicability: address product cybersecurity where relevant.
- Map adjacent legislation: inventory all external actions the agent can perform, all data it can access or generate, all systems it connects to, and all natural persons whose rights it can affect.
- Conduct the applicable conformity assessment: prepare evidence

EU Regulators Accept Temu Compliance Plan After DSA Breaches
The European Commission has accepted an action plan from Temu aimed at resolving several violations of the bloc's Digital Services Act, according to Euronews. The Chinese online retailer has committed to conducting a risk analysis, monitoring measures intended to prevent illegal products from being sold on its platform, and increasing its efforts where necessary.
Temu will also examine how its recommender systems could amplify the spread of illegal goods, the Commission indicated. The approval follows a EUR200 million fine imposed on Temu in May of this year for permitting the sale of illegal products, including dangerous baby toys and faulty chargers, on its platform.
That penalty came after a formal investigation opened in October 2024 into whether Temu was meeting its obligations as a designated Very Large Online Platform under the EU's Digital Services Act. Commission investigators found that the platform had failed to properly identify and address the risks posed by illegal and unsafe products sold to European consumers.
Temu welcomed the regulators' approval of its plan. The company said it appreciated the Commission's constructive engagement throughout the process and described the plan as evidence of its commitment to investing in robust compliance infrastructure so that EU users have a safe and trustworthy shopping environment.
The retailer has 130 million users across the 27-nation EU, nearly a third of the bloc's population, making it one of the largest online retailers in Europe. Temu is among several ecommerce platforms subject to the EU's new EUR3 fees on low-value packages since July, while goods worth less than EUR150 had previously entered the bloc duty free. The new packaging rules have coincided with a 30% to 40% slump in imports, particularly from China, since taking effect.

articles.title: European Union Debates Funding Gap for Ukraine - Defense Security Monitor
articles.summary: European Union Debates Funding Gap for Ukraine  Defense Security Monitor
articles.full_text:
When European leaders meet next month to debate further assistance to Ukraine, they will be confronted with a looming €70 billion hole in Kyiv’s finances and few good options to fill it. The need to rearm their own militaries, paired with a challenging economic environment, has strained the room for further assistance to Ukraine, while Belgium continues to oppose the conversion of frozen Russian assets into a loan.
Beyond developments on the battlefield, a key element of Ukraine’s defense is its ability to manage its finances. Kyiv’s Western partners have been crucial in helping the country plug its budget deficit, allocating over €170 billion ($189.5 billion) in financial support to Ukraine since 2022, according to the Kiel Institute.
With the U.S. curtailing aid to Ukraine under the second Trump administration, much of the assistance burden is now being shouldered by the European Union, along with Canada, Japan, Norway, and the United Kingdom.
Earlier in 2026, the E.U. approved a two-year loan plan that will provide a total of €90 billion to Ukraine over 2026 and 2027, of which €60 billion is for use on arms procurement and €30 billion is for budgetary support. Around €14 billion has been disbursed to date, and by year-end that figure should grow to €45 billion. The second half of the loan will be disbursed next year, but Ukraine’s rising needs – especially in the wake of Russian attacks on its critical infrastructure – mean that there is still a gap of around €70 billion for 2027.
European Fiscal Squeeze
So where might Europe get the remaining funds that Kyiv is seeking?
E.U. members themselves are squeezed. Concerns about Moscow’s long-term intentions in Europe and Washington’s reliability have spurred European capitals to get serious about their defense postures, driving an upswing in military expenditure.
In 2021, on the eve of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, average NATO European defense spending stood at around 1.6 percent of GDP, well below NATO’s target at the time of 2.0 percent. That figure has now risen to 2.5 percent of GDP, as the value of European defense spending has roughly doubled. At the Alliance’s 2025 summit, NATO committed to raising ‘core’ defense expenditure to 3.5 percent of GDP over the next decade.
At the same time, the E.U. as a whole is facing rising debt burdens and slowing economies. Eurozone countries have an average debt-to-GDP ratio of nearly 89 percent, while in the E.U. generally, that figure stands at close to 83 percent. Buffeted by trade wars and the Iran-related energy price shock, eurozone economies will grow only 1.1 percent in 2026, the International Monetary Fund projected earlier in October. The situation is not uniform, as some northern members of the E.U. are in much better fiscal shape than their southern and western counterparts.
The budget picture is getting cloudier. Annual inflation in the eurozone rose to 3.8 percent in September, according to Eurostat, well above the European Central Bank (ECB) target of 2 percent. The ECB has already raised interest rates twice in 2026, at the June and September meetings, and is expected to deliver another hike at one of the two remaining meetings before the end of the year. Rising prices may force the ECB to continue tightening policy, raising debt service payments from government budgets.
Supporting Ukraine remains broadly popular in the E.U., but the challenging economic environment makes it a tough sell for governments to significantly increase aid to Ukraine while also ramping up their own defense spending. European governments are already facing domestic criticism over rearmament. Italy, for example, was approved for an allocation of up to €14.9 billion from the E.U.’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) loan facility, meant to aid rearmament. Yet Rome requested only about €8 billion from SAFE, as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government sparred with critics within her own coalition and in the opposition on financing more defense spending with debt.
Frozen Russian Assets
E.U. countries are thus once again looking at alternative methods of backstopping Ukraine’s budget. One of the most obvious options is the conversion of frozen Russian financial assets into a loan.
In 2022, following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the G7 took steps to freeze Russian government securities held abroad. As much as $300 billion was impounded as a result and remains in limbo to this day, including about €210 billion held in the European financial system.
While the principal has remained untouched, the E.U. has gradually taken steps to utilize the interest income on those securities for assistance to Ukraine, on the grounds that Russia, as aggressor, should pay for the damage caused to Ukraine. That process has generated about €8 billion in windfall profits, of which €3.8 billion has been delivered to Ukraine, and €4.2 billion has been reserved to repay E.U. or G7 loans to Ukraine.
In September, Germany and other E.U. members revived the topic of converting the Russian assets into a loan for Kyiv, POLITICO reported. Berlin views the step as a ‘win-win’ for the E.U., enabling the bloc to help Kyiv address its financial needs, while replacing some of the funds that would be reserved for Ukraine in the E.U.’s upcoming multi-year budget.
The politics around seizing the Russian assets, however, have hardly changed, meaning this route likely faces a dead-end.
Belgium is the custodian of much of those Russian funds, which are housed in the Brussels-based Euroclear, and the Belgian government fears that it would bear the legal and financial risk alone. Earlier in 2026, the Bank of Russia filed a lawsuit in Moscow demanding the release of the funds from Euroclear, arguing that they were illegally seized. The court backed the Russian central bank’s challenge in a ruling two months later, though it lacks jurisdiction to enforce the judgment.
Concern over the legal risks resulted in Belgium blocking the previous attempt to repurpose Russia’s frozen assets in 2025, and will likely stymie the proposal again.
“I am certain that the European Commission will not make proposals to meet Ukraine’s financing needs through a new operation linked to Russian assets,” Belgian Prime Minister Bart de Wever told reporters on October 21. “I am certain of that, because that is what was said.”
Rising Urgency as the War Enters Its Sixth Year
European leaders are due to meet toward the end of November to iron out assistance to Ukraine for next year. Ahead of this summit, the E.U. is also looking to push other partners to increase their contributions to Kyiv. Unless additional funding can be found, from either new aid commitments or a change of policy on the frozen Russian assets, Ukraine will enter the new year with a sizable financial gap.
The situation is meanwhile becoming more urgent. Ukraine has largely exhausted its stockpile of air-defense interceptors, leaving its cities and energy grid vulnerable to Russian missile attacks. Earlier in October, Ukrainian military intelligence agency HUR estimated that Russia can produce 10,000 long-range strike drones and decoys each month. Mounting damage increases Ukraine’s financial needs, as the country scrambles to keep the lights on.
In February, the war will enter its sixth year with no resolution in sight. The longer the conflict lasts, the more its outcome will hinge on financing as much as firepower.

articles.title: Ukraine improves jet-powered drone interception rates, but Starlink disruptions threaten progress - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Ukraine improves jet-powered drone interception rates, but Starlink disruptions threaten progress  Euronews.comUkraine’s Drones Have Eliminated or Wounded an Army of 300,000 Russians in Less Than a Year  UNITED24 MediaUkraine intercepting more Russian Geran-4 jet-powered drones, General Staff says  The Kyiv IndependentAir defenses neutralize two ballistic missiles, 255 drones in overnight Russian attack on Ukraine  UkrinformOvercoming the jet-powered Geran...
articles.full_text:
Ukraine made significant progress in countering Russia's jet-powered drones, with some air defence units reporting interception rates around 80%. But recent restrictions on US satellite services exposed Kyiv's reliance on US technology as it races to develop cheaper, more effective interceptors.
Ukraine's improved interceptor drone technology has helped it counter Russia's jet-powered drones, but disruptions to US Starshield satellite services threaten those gains.
According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), Ukraine's interception rate fell slightly from 77% to around 74% during disruptions to the military-grade satellite service between 14 and 24 October.
The figures nevertheless represent a marked improvement on early September, when Ukrainian officials reported intercepting around 60% of Russia's jet-powered drones.
Some Ukrainian air defence units have reported interception rates exceeding 80%, although these figures reflect individual units' performance rather than nationwide results.
The Starshield restrictions, which affected high-speed drone operations, were lifted on 24 October, according to Ukrainian officials. However, the disruption highlighted the country's dependence on US satellite communications to sustain its air defences.
ISW warned that maintaining and improving interception rates would require Ukraine to develop and deploy affordable, high-speed interceptor drones on a much larger scale.
Russia has increasingly turned to jet-powered versions of its Shahed-type attack drones, which travel considerably faster than conventional propeller-driven models, leaving Ukrainian air defence crews with significantly less time to detect and intercept them.
Ukraine relies on a combination of interceptor drones, fighter aircraft and ground-based systems to counter the threat.
Interceptor drones have proved particularly effective, according to ISW, but many depend on Starshield connectivity to operate at the speeds required to engage faster Russian targets.
Ukrainian forces also use F-16 fighter jets, either firing air-to-air missiles or engaging targets with onboard guns. Both approaches have drawbacks: missiles are expensive and scarce, while gun engagements demand considerable pilot skill and expose aircraft and crews to additional risks.
Using fighter jets against drones also increases maintenance requirements and diverts aircraft from other missions.
Ukraine has installed ground-based gun turrets in Kyiv and the surrounding region, although expanding these systems nationwide would require considerable time and resources.
The race for cheaper interceptors
The growing threat has accelerated efforts by Ukrainian manufacturers to develop faster, more affordable interception systems.
One such project is the F-Jet 80, a jet-powered interceptor being developed by Ukrainian company F-Drones, which plans to incorporate artificial intelligence into its guidance system.
The company aims to keep the unit cost at approximately $7,000, compared with an estimated $20,000 to $70,000 for other high-speed interceptor drones and around $1 million for an air-to-air missile launched from an F-16.
Although the F-Jet 80 remains under development, its manufacturer says it has already successfully intercepted several Russian drones.
For Ukraine, the challenge extends beyond developing effective technology to producing it in sufficient numbers to counter Russia's expanding use of jet-powered drones.
ISW argues that integrating affordable interceptor drones into Ukraine's existing air defence network offers the strongest prospect of sustaining high interception rates as the country approaches another winter of Russian aerial attacks.

U.S. President Donald Trump is considering lifting sanctions against Russia's government investment fund, the New York Times reported Oct. 27, citing an unnamed U.S. official.
The White House is assessing how sanctions may be lifted against the fund to improve bilateral relations with Moscow and help end Russia's war against Ukraine, the official said.
Russian officials have also pushed for U.S. sanctions against the investment fund to be lifted because of the financial structure's involvement with Trump's diesel deal with Russia, people familiar with the matter told the New York Times.
On Oct. 9, Trump said that Russia had agreed to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets following a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," he wrote on Truth Social.
The first ship carrying 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel then set sail en route to New York, expected to arrive in early November, Reuters reported Oct. 23, citing London Stock Exchange Group data.
The Malta-flagged tanker loaded its cargo in the Russian Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct. 22 and is set to arrive in the U.S. on Nov. 7, according to the outlet.
read also
Ukrainian officials also fear the White House could explore a deal involving Russia's fertilizer industry, two people familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent in an article published Oct. 23.
The proposal would fit an approach in which the U.S. offers Russia economic benefits in hopes of persuading Moscow to end its war, one U.S. government official and one Senate official said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 23 that a new round of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. is expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi a possible venue.
On Oct. 25, Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told state-controlled media that the Kremlin is ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the U.S. after Nov. 4, when Russia celebrates National Unity Day.
As the U.S. considers lifting sanctions, Russia continues to launch missiles and drone attacks against civilian infrastructure in cities across Ukraine.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a deadly attack overnight on Oct. 26-27, striking a university campus, a major bridge, an administrative building, and medical facilities.

articles.title: Rosebank oilfield would not breach UK emission targets, say government insiders - The Guardian
articles.summary: Rosebank oilfield would not breach UK emission targets, say government insiders  The GuardianPolitical battle intensifies within Labour over Rosebank oil field  BBCBudget assumes approval of Rosebank oilfield despite cabinet split  The TimesHealey backs oil drilling at Rosebank  The TelegraphUK Weighs Scrapping Its Largest Untapped Oilfield With Oil Over $100  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
articles.full_text:
The giant Rosebank oilfield can be approved without breaching the UK’s emission targets, according to government insiders, in a boost to those in the cabinet who are pushing for it to be given the go-ahead.
The Guardian revealed last week that Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, was leaning towards rejecting the project, but her position has put her at loggerheads with cabinet colleagues, including the chancellor, John Healey, who are lobbying for an approval.
Government insiders have told the Guardian the project can be approved on a strict reading of Britain’s climate obligations, in part because once the oil is exported, the emissions from burning it no longer count against domestic targets. “Miatta has more latitude than you might think,” said one.
A decision to approve the oilfield would be met with dismay from climate campaigners and some Labour backbenchers who view it as a harmful step away from prioritising net zero – and may see the shift of emissions from one country to another as a trivial distinction.
On Tuesday, Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth wrote to the prime minister urging him to consider the cumulative impacts of big decisions on North Sea drilling, Heathrow expansion and grants for heat pumps – rather than viewing each in isolation.
But sources say the Treasury has already accounted for billions of pounds’ worth of tax revenue from Rosebank and so would be faced with a shortfall should it be rejected.
“The climate case against was never the direct emissions,” one source said. “Instead it was the leadership position … the power of a G7 producer seeking to put that into action is the climate point, not the direct emissions.”
Greg Muttitt, a climate researcher at University College, London, said the government was wrong to approve the Jackdaw gasfield last week and would be wrong to approve Rosebank, which would generate around seven times the emissions.
But he added: “It is true that the UK government is not going to find itself in any international court if it approves Rosebank. Approving it is not inconsistent with what the UK has committed to firmly, because most of the oil will be exported and so will count towards other countries’ emissions.”
Fahnbulleh has been forced to make a decision over Rosebank because of a legal judgment that the previous environmental consent was incorrectly given by the Conservative government at the time.
A judge ruled in 2024 that ministers should have accounted for emissions not just from drilling for oil at Rosebank, but also from those which will be generated by burning it.
Given most of that oil will be burned abroad, however, the resulting emissions will not count against the UK’s carbon budgets. Experts estimate that Rosebank could emit 1m additional tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2042, against an overall limit of 90m tonnes.
Fahnbulleh is under an obligation to take into account Britain’s commitment under the Paris agreement to take action to prevent global temperatures rising more than 1.5C.
In her decision to approve the Jackdaw scheme last week, however, she noted Jackdaw would account for about 0.01% of global greenhouse gas emissions created by the oil and gas industry in 2035.
Some experts believe Rosebank could be approved without meaningfully adding to global temperature changes. But others insist that any new oil and gasfields are harmful to the goal of staying within safe carbon budgets.
Downing Street insiders insist the decision rests with Fahnbulleh, rather than with Andy Burnham. However supportive ministers have interpreted the prime minister’s promise to take a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas as a signal he would support giving the green light to Rosebank.
He has also talked of “reindustrialisation” in a speech in Motherwell, North Lanarkshire, this month, language often associated in Scotland with the North Sea. Scottish Labour MPs are believed to be overwhelmingly in favour of approving the oilfield.
Fahnbulleh told the Guardian last week that while she had approved the Jackdaw gasfield on the grounds of national energy security, the same concerns did not necessarily apply to Rosebank.
Her allies say she is leaning away from approving it because the climate damage it would create, while arguably not enough to violate legal limits, would not be overriden by the potential benefits, which those who support its approval argue includes tax take, jobs and investment.
In recent days, however, people close to the chancellor have said he wants Fahnbulleh to approve the project.
The Guardian has learned that part of the reason for this is the Treasury has already accounted for the tax benefits, which Adura, the company operating the field, estimate would be £500m a year by the end of this parliament.
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Any decision will be made through the quasi-judicial process, taking into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received as part of the regulatory process.”

articles.title: Thirteen Rules: Researchers Say the EU and UK Hold the Levers to Rein In AI - Bioengineer.org
articles.summary: Thirteen Rules: Researchers Say the EU and UK Hold the Levers to Rein In AI  Bioengineer.org
articles.full_text:
As European and British leaders prepare to meet in Brussels on 20 November for the second EU-UK summit, a group of seventeen researchers has published a white paper arguing that artificial intelligence must be added to the agenda. The announced programme for the summit, hosted by António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, covers defence, energy, agrifood rules, climate and migration. Yet despite recent reports of AI agents breaking out of their test environments, and an open letter from more than 1,100 industry employees asking governments to apply brakes, the technology is not on the table. The new paper, written by researchers from the universities of Sussex, Cambridge, Bologna, Macerata and Innsbruck, the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, the Max Planck Society, the Hasso Plattner Institute, the German Environment Agency and civil society organisations, contends that the time for AI regulation is now, and that Europe should lead. It sets out thirteen rules that EU and UK governments should advance.
The paper’s central argument is that the public debate has been too narrow. According to Jochen Büttner, coauthor from the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, the AI debate revolves around safety, and the white paper agrees that red lines on models must be established and that liability for the companies publishing them must be enforced. But, he argues, this focus overlooks the fact that the most widespread harms of AI are fiscal and physical, and that AI companies are already harming people. The document therefore pairs the familiar safety agenda with two domains that regulators have treated far more lightly: the tax code and the environment. Its authors describe a technology sector that rewards the replacement of workers with software and that consumes land, water and fossil energy at a scale that local communities and national regulators are struggling to constrain.
The fiscal case rests on a structural mismatch. Tax systems were designed for an economy in which value comes from wages. In the United States, effective tax rates range from 25.5 to 33.5 percent on labour but sit at roughly 5 percent on equipment and software. Across the OECD, labour supplies about 57 percent of tax revenue while capital contributes about 19 percent. When a company replaces people with software, it cuts both its wage bill and its tax bill, and the public purse loses twice: once in revenue and again in the cost of supporting displaced workers. The exposure is large. The International Labour Organization estimates that one in four jobs worldwide, and 34 percent of jobs in high-income countries, is in an occupation exposed to generative AI. The white paper proposes ending tax rules that favour automation over employment, introducing a usage-based levy on compute, and returning part of the value of appropriated data to the public.
Jürgen Renn, another coauthor from the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, frames the risk in blunt terms. The fiscal base, he says, is shifting from labour to capital faster than tax authorities can follow, and without reform AI will be paid for by cuts to the very services that cushion AI-generated unemployment and job insecurity. The paper’s taxation rule translates this diagnosis into legislative instruments. It calls for an end to tax treatment favouring automation over employment, a usage-based levy on compute or tokens collected on the destination principle, and a levy on data appropriation feeding a public fund. The proposed legal vehicles include member-state tax law with EU coordination, a UK Finance Bill modelled on the Digital Services Tax, and OECD frameworks.
The environmental chapter documents a sector moving in the opposite direction to its own earlier promises. Digital technology once promised dematerialisation: less paper, fewer journeys, smarter grids. The AI boom, the authors argue, goes the other way. On 6 October, a Finnish agency ordered Google’s local subsidiary to halt work at two data-centre sites after about 300 hectares of forest had been cleared without permission. In the United States, xAI runs about 1.5 gigawatts of gas turbines in Memphis, Meta has committed to ten gas-fired plants for its Louisiana campus, and 59 data-centre projects have announced some 90 gigawatts of onsite generation built on gas turbines and engines. In Spain, two thirds of data centres have water demand exceeding local supply in parts of the year. The International Energy Agency reports that data-centre electricity demand rose 17 percent in 2025, against 3 percent for electricity demand overall.
The United Kingdom, the paper notes, is accelerating consent for data centres in AI Growth Zones without binding conditions on efficiency, water or waste heat. The authors ask why big technology companies escape requirements that local European firms have always faced, and they answer with two regulatory proposals. The first is environmental limits on compute: data-centre consent and grid connection should be granted only with additional renewable supply, a power usage effectiveness of at most 1.2 and minimum waste-heat reuse, with consent withheld where impacts cannot be assessed. The proposed legal vehicles include Germany’s Energy Efficiency Act thresholds applied as permit conditions, the Irish grid-connection rule, planned EU minimum performance standards for 2027, and the UK National Policy Statement for data centres. The second is mandatory life-cycle disclosure: public energy and water figures per facility and per model, across training and inference, including upstream mining and electronic waste, achieved by amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 to move from confidential filing to publication and by extending the Energy Efficiency Directive’s Article 12.
Why Europe, and why now? The paper argues that the EU and UK together account for roughly a quarter of global AI demand, and that the so-called Brussels effect shows conditions attached to the common European market tend to become global corporate standards. The supply side matters too: every leading-edge AI chip is printed with lithography made only by ASML in the Netherlands, with optics provided by Carl Zeiss. Since 2 August, the European Commission has held enforcement powers over general-purpose AI models, and on 21 September it opened a consultation on minimum performance standards for data centres. The white paper’s conclusion is that the EU already has the legislative backbone and must now strengthen it in collaboration with the UK, rather than treat regulation as a purely American safety debate.
The thirteen rules are organised around one overarching instrument and twelve substantive measures spanning democracy, labour and equity, planetary health and safety. The centrepiece is a licence to operate for general-purpose AI in both the EU and the UK: no certificate, no market, with access conditional on demonstrated compliance and tightening on a published schedule, and exports of EUV lithography made conditional on downstream compliance. This would be implemented through Articles 51(2) and 97 of the AI Act by delegated act, the UK’s frontier AI bill, and Article 4 of the Dual-Use Regulation. Further rules address gatekeeping oversight, requiring fair ranking in AI answers, no self-preferencing and auditable retrieval logs, plus remuneration for authors whose works trained the models, using an extended Digital Markets Act Article 6(5), the UK’s digital markets conduct requirements and a review of the CDSM Directive. Competition rules would introduce systemic-importance designations keyed to compute share, merger approval conditional on open access, and procurement that rewards capability-extending AI.
Labour provisions call for human review of algorithmic pay and dismissal decisions, collective bargaining for data and moderation workers, and due diligence reaching contractors abroad, drawing on the Platform Work Directive and the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive. The safety rules retain the familiar red lines on containment escape, deception and shutdown resistance, pre-deployment evaluations with regulator-set thresholds in isolated environments, and liability resting with the model provider, implemented through AI Act Articles 5 and 55, statutory access for AI safety institutes and the Product Liability Directive. A final implementation rule would complete the standards layer and create a European AI Impact Observatory independent of the AI Office, using AI Act Articles 40, 41 and 68. The authors call on EU and UK leaders to add AI to the summit declaration, to agree a joint licence to operate, and to carry common standards for data centres and taxation into the UK’s G20 presidency in 2027.
The paper is published as a commentary rather than an empirical study, and its proposals are advocacy positions rather than evaluated policies. Its lead author, Felix Creutzig of the Bennett Institute at the University of Sussex, summarises the argument: Europe discusses AI as if the only question were safety in Silicon Valley, while the harm closer to home is a tax system that rewards replacing people with software and a digital sector that used to be green and is turning black, with forests cleared in Finland and gas turbines in Memphis. The 20 November summit, the authors argue, is the opportunity to put the rules on the table.

articles.title: European Commission approves Temu plan to follow EU rules after €200m fine - BurgasMedia
articles.summary: European Commission approves Temu plan to follow EU rules after €200m fine  BurgasMedia
articles.full_text:
The European Commission has approved Temu's plan to comply with the Digital Services Act, five months after fining the Chinese platform €200m ($233m). The Commission announced the decision on 26 October.
Temu now has four months to file an interim risk assessment, which must show that the steps in the plan are already in place. It covers a six-month period ending on 30 November 2026.
Temu is a Chinese online retail platform. The Digital Services Act (DSA) classes it as a very large online platform. It has 130m users in the EU's 27 countries, almost a third of the population, and is one of the biggest retailers in Europe.
The plan has five parts, all of them corrective steps. They include a risk assessment made specifically for Temu, using reliable, up-to-date data on the risks from the platform's design, how it works and how people use it.
The plan also adds reliable indicators to measure whether the steps limit the spread of illegal content.
Temu must also review gaps in the checks it runs on content itself, before anyone reports a problem, including how those gaps affect recommended products. The review covers the platform's rules, moderation rules, automatic detection tools, manual checks, feedback systems and how it divides its resources.
A further check will look at whether the systems that recommend products, and other algorithms, can boost the spread of illegal content.
The last part is an analysis of deliberate manipulation of the service and of how illegal content could spread quickly and widely. It must also show how sellers and other users could use the platform's features to list illegal products.
The Commission says Temu will closely monitor the steps against the sale of illegal goods and step up its efforts if needed. The plan was first reviewed by the Board of national digital services regulators, and the Commission then made the decision.
The Commission opened a formal investigation into Temu in October 2024. It sent the company its preliminary findings in July 2025. The non-compliance decision, with the fine, came on 28 May 2026. The deadline for the plan was 28 August, and Temu filed it in August.
Commission investigators say Temu failed to properly identify or tackle the risks from illegal and unsafe products sold to European consumers. Its 2024 risk assessment relied on general data about online shopping, not evidence about the platform itself. As a result, the Commission says, the company underestimated the chance that EU shoppers would come across illegal products.
The Commission also says Temu did not properly assess how its recommendation algorithms and its influencer promotion programme could spread illegal products.
Test purchases by an independent lab showed that many chargers fail basic safety checks. Several baby toys were rated "medium to high" risk because of banned chemicals and small parts a child could choke on.
"Risk assessments are not a box-ticking exercise. They are the backbone of the DSA," Henna Virkkunen, the Commission's executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, said in May.
Temu disputes the fine as disproportionate. The company says the case is about its first risk assessment, from 2024, and does not reflect its current systems.
Temu welcomed the approval of the plan. It says the plan shows its commitment to invest in solid compliance infrastructure to give all users in the EU a safe and trusted place to shop. "We appreciate the Commission's constructive engagement with us throughout the process," Temu said in a statement.
Under the DSA, big platforms can be fined up to 6% of their global annual turnover. If they fail to follow Commission decisions, they can also face periodic penalty payments.
In July, the Commission also fined AliExpress €550m, the biggest fine under the law so far.
Since July, the EU has charged a €3 fee on low-value parcels. Before that, parcels worth under €150 came in duty-free. Temu is among the platforms hit by the fee. Since the new rules, imports, especially from China, have fallen by 30% to 40%.

Germany has been seeking to diversify its strategic and trade links to counter the perceived unreliability of the US or China’s growth as an economic rival.
Speaking in Singapore, the first stop of a visit that will also take him to Japan and South Korea, Merz said there were “no uncertainties in Europe”.
“Under the federal government I lead, investment opportunities will be continuously improved,” Merz said after meeting Singapore prime minister Lawrence Wong.
“All I can say is that I encounter a great deal of confidence here in Germany and in Europe as locations for investment.”
The German leader’s comments came despite fresh turbulence in Berlin, where his government has faced pressure — including the resignation this month of a key minister from its junior coalition partner.
Merz’s approval ratings have also weakened, while support for the far right has risen.
Elsewhere in Europe, France has seen widespread looting and protests over the past weeks.
But Singapore’s Wong said investor confidence remained high in Germany and Europe.
“Our investors are long-term investors. They are not just investing for one election cycle,” he said.
“Singapore believes in the longer term potential of Germany and Europe.”
‘Common interests’
Experts say Germany viewed the democracies of Japan and South Korea and the business-friendly city-state of Singapore as like-minded partners.
Those nations had “common interests”, Merz said.
“If we undertake these efforts together, then our independence from other countries will grow significantly,” he said, without naming specific nations.
But in a speech, delivered later on Tuesday, Merz said the EU’s view on China has become “more nuanced”.
“China’s pivotal role in world politics raises deep questions regarding trade, security and international order,” he said.
Beijing is Germany’s top economic partner in Asia and has long been a major investment destination, but is also seen as a growing competitor.
“Wise China policy begins at home. This principle holds true in the Indo-Pacific as much as in Europe,” Merz said.
“We will be better equipped to build balanced relations with China if we ourselves are united, strong, resilient, innovative and competitive.”
The German leader will fly to Japan on Wednesday, where he will meet Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and visit South Korea on Thursday and Friday.
In South Korea, Merz will meet President Lee Jae Myung and visit the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea.

articles.title: From Fiber Blend to Forest Plot: How Pellet Producers Can Prepare for EUDR - Biomass Magazine
articles.summary: From Fiber Blend to Forest Plot: How Pellet Producers Can Prepare for EUDR  Biomass Magazine
articles.full_text:
October 27, 2026
BY Timothy Daniel
For years, wood pellet producers have managed traceability through a familiar combination of supplier files, sustainability certifications, spreadsheets, scale tickets, bills of lading and audit binders. This approach has been workable because most reporting frameworks allowed for batch-level, supplier-level or certification-based evidence.
The EU Deforestation Regulation raises that standard considerably. As of October 2026, the regulation is scheduled to take effect on Dec. 30 for large and medium operators, and for micro and small operators already covered by the EU Timber Regulation. Most other micro and small operators have until June 30, 2027. Wood pellets fall squarely within scope, as EUDR covers wood products under heading 4401, including sawdust, wood waste and scrap agglomerated into pellets or similar forms.
The core requirement is simple to state but considerably harder to operationalize: Relevant products placed on or exported from the EU market must be deforestation-free, legally produced and supported by documented due diligence. For wood products, this means demonstrating that the material did not originate from land affected by deforestation or forest degradation after Dec. 31, 2020, and that it was harvested in accordance with the laws of the country of production.
Where Traceability Breaks Down 
Pellets are typically manufactured from blended inputs—sawdust, chips, shavings, residue and other low-grade fiber sourced from multiple suppliers, mills and harvest areas. Once these materials enter storage, drying and pelletizing, it becomes increasingly difficult to connect a finished pellet shipment back to the specific supplier records, harvest dates, species information, legality evidence and geolocation data that due diligence requires.
For this reason, EUDR readiness is best understood not as a last-mile reporting task, but as a data infrastructure problem.
A producer preparing for EUDR needs to determine, for each EU-bound shipment, what fiber went into it, where that fiber originated, whether the origin plots are supported by defensible geolocation evidence, whether legality records are complete and whether any risk indicators require mitigation. When this information is dispersed across email inboxes, PDFs, spreadsheets, ERP exports, scale systems and supplier portals, compliance teams can spend more time locating and reconciling data than actually evaluating risk.
Geolocation Requirements Under EUDR 
Geolocation data constitutes a mandatory component of EUDR compliance. Each Due Diligence Statement submitted under the regulation must establish a direct link between the relevant commodity and the specific land parcel from which it originated. 
Advertisement
Geolocation requirements vary by plot size: 
● Plots of 4 hectares or less: A single set of coordinates (latitude and longitude, expressed to a minimum of six decimal places) is sufficient to satisfy the geolocation requirement.
● Plots exceeding 4 hectares: A single coordinate point is insufficient. These plots must instead be represented by a polygon—a series of connected coordinate points delineating the complete outer boundary of the plot.
● Cattle: Irrespective of the size of the area involved, cattle-related submissions require only point coordinates identifying the establishment where the animals were kept. Polygon data is not required in this case.
Regardless of the format in which spatial data is initially collected—including shapefiles (SHP), KML files or raw coordinate data, such data must ultimately be converted into GeoJSON format prior to submission, as this is the only format currently accepted by the EU's Information System.
For pellet producers, this requirement adds a layer of complexity beyond document collection. Harvest areas feeding a single production run may span dozens of plots across multiple suppliers, some above the four-hectare threshold and some below it. Each must be resolved to the correct geolocation format, validated and preserved in a form that can be retrieved and defended years after the shipment has left the mill.
Where AI and Automation Can Help 
This is where AI and automation can provide meaningful support, provided they are applied to the right problem.
Take Rimba, for example—an AI-native operational compliance platform that helps pellet producers continuously monitor, track and report on their operations to meet the standards set by EUDR. Rimba's role is not to replace legal judgment or sustainability programs. It is to help industrial teams convert fragmented operational, geolocation and supply chain data into structured, traceable, report-ready records. The platform is built for heavy industry workflows in which critical information arrives in many formats, including PDFs, spreadsheets, emails, invoices, bills of lading, scale tickets, sustainability declarations, production data, shapefiles, KML and others.
For pellet producers, this kind of automation can support several EUDR readiness steps.
First, producers need better supplier data intake. Rather than manually collecting documents and retyping fields into spreadsheets, an AI-driven workflow can extract key information from supplier declarations, harvest documents, transport records and invoices. It can normalize supplier names, dates, product types, quantities and origin data so that teams are not continually reconciling mismatched file formats.
Second, producers need chain-of-custody continuity. When a truckload of sawdust is received from a sawmill, that intake record should be connected to supplier documentation, geolocation evidence, batch allocation and eventual pellet output. Rimba can help establish a single operational record spanning documents and systems, reducing the risk that compliance evidence becomes separated from the physical material it is meant to support.
Third, producers need automated reconciliation. EUDR compliance depends on consistency: Quantities on purchase orders should match scale tickets, shipments should align with inventory movements and batch records should correspond to supplier claims. Rimba's reconciliation workflows can flag discrepancies early, before they become audit findings or shipment delays.
Fourth, producers need risk visibility. Missing or incomplete geolocation data is one of the most common gaps: a plot recorded as a single point when it exceeds 4 hectares and requires a full polygon, a coordinate submitted with insufficient decimal precision, or a file delivered in SHP or KML format that was never converted to GeoJSON. Alongside incomplete legality documents, unusual supplier activity or mismatched volumes, these are issues that should not be discovered days before export. Automated monitoring can surface such gaps as they emerge, giving procurement, sustainability and operations teams time to resolve issues with suppliers before they affect a shipment.
Finally, producers need audit-ready reporting. EUDR requires companies to retain due diligence records for five years. This means the value of a compliance system lies not only in whether it can produce a report today, but in whether it can demonstrate how the company reached its conclusions later. A robust system should preserve source documents, data transformations, reconciliation history and human review decisions.
A Familiar Pattern, at a Sharper Standard 
The pellet industry has already navigated overlapping sustainability expectations, including certification schemes, greenhouse gas reporting, chain-of-custody audits and renewable energy market requirements. EUDR introduces a sharper traceability standard, but it also fits a broader pattern: buyers, regulators and auditors increasingly expect companies to substantiate their claims with underlying data.
AI-native platforms can serve as the connective layer across this process, bridging the messy reality of industrial data with the structured evidence regulators expect. Rather than requiring teams to chase documents across inboxes and spreadsheets, such platforms help build a reliable compliance record spanning procurement, production and shipment.
Author: Timothy Daniel 
Cofounder and CEO, Rimba
