articles.title: The Netherlands defies Europe’s tech trend thanks to ASML - ing think
articles.summary: The Netherlands defies Europe’s tech trend thanks to ASML  ing think
articles.full_text:
While Europe has lagged the US and Asia in capitalising on the global tech boom, the Netherlands stands out as an exception. ASML and its semiconductor equipment give the Dutch economy a unique position in the global AI investment boom, with an economic footprint that could reach 2.2% in 2026
- The Netherlands stands out in Europe for its ability to benefit from the global tech boom thanks to ASML and the semiconductor-equipment cluster.
- ASML has become a macroeconomic force in its own right: its direct contribution could reach 1.6% of Dutch value-added in 2026.
- Its true economic footprint is even larger. Including domestic suppliers and investment, we estimate ASML’s contribution could reach 2.2% in 2026.
- The benefits go beyond current GDP: ASML’s highly productive ecosystem may generate wider productivity spillovers across the Dutch economy.
- Success also creates concentration risk. ASML’s growing weight means semiconductor swings can increasingly affect Dutch economic growth.
- Geopolitics could hinder growth through restrictions on export markets and disruptions to critical foreign inputs.
- Constraints may also be domestic: shortages of talent, space and other supply-side bottlenecks could limit further rapid growth of the cluster.
The Dutch economy is profiting from the strong global tech cycle
The Netherlands is an exception to Europe's difficulty in capturing the full benefits of the global tech boom. According to the IMF's latest World Economic Outlook, the Netherlands is among the countries most exposed to the global AI investment cycle through trade, a trend that is boosting growth across the economies involved.
This is predominantly due to the strength of computer chip equipment maker ASML and the wider semiconductor ecosystem surrounding it. ASML has rapidly become the largest European company by market capitalisation and is becoming a dominant force in the Dutch economic outlook. In fact, changes in turnover expectations have become valuable insights for the Dutch near-term economic outlook.
Mario Draghi has warned that Europe risks becoming trapped in older technologies. Yet thanks to ASML and the ecosystem around it, the Netherlands occupies a pivotal position in the AI-driven technology boom and is reaping substantial economic benefits from it.
In this note, we quantify the ASML impact on the Dutch economy and discuss its implications. We argue that ASML’s importance to the global economy has helped cushion the impact of shocks such as the energy crisis and recent trade tensions in the Netherlands. We also argue that it is set to boost the Dutch economic outlook, and while it comes with certain vulnerabilities, it is a key driver of modernisation and productivity growth in the years to come.
Share of machinery in the Dutch economy has accelerated in the last 10 years thanks to ASML
Already familiar to industry experts and increasingly recognised by the broader public, ASML is a Dutch company and the world's sole producer of leading-edge lithography tools essential for advanced semiconductor manufacturing.
Developing these advanced technologies requires substantial R&D expenditure. As there are not yet competitive alternatives to its most advanced lithography tools, this gives ASML a strong position in price negotiations. That makes ASML quite profitable. However, customer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company has recently shown some reluctance to adopt ASML’s newest technology, initially viewing the tools as too costly, highlighting that the company’s pricing power has its limits.
Nevertheless, ASML generates substantial value-added (see below for our methodology on how we estimate the direct value-added contribution and the wider impact for the Dutch economy). While the company is a multinational, its main production and R&D activities are based in the Netherlands. As a result, it is mostly Dutch GDP that is boosted by the expansion of ASML.[1]
ASML's rise is clearly visible in industry data. Since 2017, the share of machinery in total Dutch gross value-added has increased. Trends like the introduction and increasing popularity of smartphones, cloud-based services, social media and the demand boom in (ICT) goods during the Covid lockdowns have been very beneficial for semiconductor-related businesses, including producers of semiconductor lithography systems. This trend has accelerated with the rise of large language models and the broader AI investment cycle, lifting the machinery industry's share of the Dutch economy to around 2.7% in current prices and 2.9% in constant prices by 2025.
Half of the Dutch machinery industry is ASML
Admittedly, ASML is not the only machinery company in the Netherlands, and not all machinery expansion can be attributed to just this business. Other large tech companies in the semiconductor equipment manufacturing cluster include ASM International and BE Semiconductor Industries. Other well-known Dutch companies active in the wider machinery industry include VDL Groep (e.g. food, packaging, and agricultural robots, also an important supplier to ASML), Vanderlande (e.g. logistics systems) and Lely (e.g. cattle milking robots and feeding systems). Yet, ASML accounts for about half (€33.7bn in 2025) of the turnover of the Dutch machinery industry.[2]
ASML alone is on track to account for 1.6% of the Dutch economy
For each euro of turnover, ASML creates about 50 cents of value-added with its own activities, of which we (perhaps somewhat conservatively) assume that 40 cents can be assigned domestically, which is slightly less than the 42 cents of the total machinery industry.
We therefore estimate that the direct contribution of ASML to Dutch GDP has risen from a modest 0.1% in 1995 to a substantial 1.3% in 2025. That is significant for an economy with a high development level and a high degree of diversification. Based on ASML’s own expectations (of which we take the midpoint of €44.5bn) and our own economic growth forecasts, this may well be 1.6% in 2026.
Including the wider ASML ecosystem, its share of the Dutch economy is even larger
ASML's success is closely tied to the ecosystem that has developed around it. Many of its suppliers are located around Veldhoven, where ASML's headquarters are, making the broader value chain key to the company's success.
To track the wider impact of ASML (and the machinery industry) on the Dutch economy, we estimate and aggregate the following three impacts (over time):
- Direct impact: ASML’s/machinery’s own gross value-added share in total gross value-added
- Indirect impacts[3]:
2a. Domestic value-added content of intermediate consumption. This is the value-added created by other Dutch firms that supply inputs for the production of ASML/machines. In ASML's case, this may also include inputs provided by the machinery industry.
2b. Domestic value-added content of gross capital formation: This is the value-added created by other firms in the Netherlands that result from providing productive assets.
In the absence of ASML-specific data, we investigate the indirect impacts by looking into intermediate inputs and investment of the Dutch machinery industry, using input-output tables.
About half of the gross intermediate inputs come from the Netherlands, half from abroad. For each euro of total intermediate consumption by the machinery industry/ASML, about 20 cents of domestic value-added is created. This means that intermediate consumption by the total machinery industry has an impact of 0.8% of total Dutch value-added. If we scale this to the size of ASML, this means the domestic impact of intermediate consumption by ASML is 0.3% of the Dutch economy in 2025 (and is forecast at 0.4% in 2026). This is still quite sizeable.
The machinery industry sources a large share of its inputs from within the sector, although many of these suppliers are located abroad. For ASML, these include both strategic partners and external suppliers, such as ZEISS SMT in Germany, as well as subsidiaries like Cymer in San Diego. Other important suppliers include wholesale trade, metal products manufacturing, and professional services such as legal and management consultancy. Within the Netherlands, however, temporary job agencies are among the biggest beneficiaries of the sector's activity, alongside other firms in the machinery industry.
Impact via investment, especially R&D
The second indirect contribution to the economy is the domestic value-added content of gross capital formation. While the impact of ASML and the broader machinery industry through investment is smaller than that of their own production and supply-chain activity, it remains significant enough to have a meaningful effect on the Dutch economy. For 2025, we estimate the contribution through investment at 0.2% for ASML and 0.1% for the broader machinery industry. For ASML, we expect this contribution to remain at 0.2% in 2026.
This captures the economic impact generated beyond the investment that is done within machinery/ASML. Own in-house R&D is not included in this estimate since it is already included in the direct impact and would otherwise be counted twice. From our analysis based on input tables, we can conclude that when it comes to sourcing, R&D investment is the most important capital asset type for the sector: on average, this was about 57% of gross capital formation. The second- and third-most important are other machinery and equipment and computer software and databases, followed by buildings and computer hardware.
Adding the direct impact and the two indirect impacts, we estimate the total impact of the machinery industry and ASML on the Dutch economy at 3.7% in 2025 (and forecast it for ASML at 2.2% in 2026). While this falls short of the 3.8% contribution Nokia made to the Finnish economy in 2000 (excluding indirect effects), it is nevertheless highly significant.

articles.full_text:
Bilateral trade between Nigeria and France reached $4.7 billion in 2025, as businesses from both countries deepen investments across energy, infrastructure, agriculture, logistics, finance and other sectors.
Speaking during the buildup of activities for this year’s French Week, the Consul General of France in Lagos, Laurent Favier, said the growing commercial relationship reflected a shift from diplomatic intentions to concrete business transactions, supported by active engagement between the two governments and private-sector organisations.
Favier, who described Nigeria as France’s leading trading partner in sub-Saharan Africa, cited recent agreements on the development of the Gateway Deep Sea Port and the adjoining Ogun State Blue Marine Special Economic Zone as examples of expanding economic cooperation.
The agreements were advanced in Paris in September 2026 in the presence of President Tinubu, alongside broader efforts to attract investment and strengthen commercial links between the two countries.
According to Favier, over 100 French companies currently operate in Nigeria across pharmaceuticals, agriculture, insurance, logistics, transport, infrastructure and hospitality, generating roughly 14,000 direct local jobs.
He put France’s foreign direct investment stock in Nigeria at €8.1 billion in 2025, describing the investments as evidence of a long-term commitment to economic partnership and sustainable growth.
He noted that French companies, including TotalEnergies, CMA CGM, SPIE, Schneider Electric and Danone, are continuing to expand their Nigerian operations, while newer commercial developments are extending the relationship into retail, hospitality and entertainment.
Retail giant Carrefour and hospitality group Accor are among the French brands expanding their presence in Nigeria, while Canal+ has strengthened its position in the entertainment industry through its acquisition strategy involving MultiChoice.
Favier said the growing engagement reflected increasing opportunities for French businesses in Nigeria’s large consumer market and for Nigerian companies seeking access to French investors and European markets.
President of the Franco-Nigerian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI), Guillaume Niarfeix, said this year’s French Week would focus on converting discussions between businesses into concrete partnerships and investment opportunities.
The week-long programme, described by the chamber as Nigeria’s largest C-level business networking event, is scheduled to hold in Lagos from tomorrow, October 29 to November 6, 2026.
Niarfeix said French investments are visible across several strategic sectors, including energy, transport and logistics, with projects expected to support infrastructure development and economic activity.
In the energy sector, he cited TotalEnergies’ 2024 final investment decision with the Nigerian National Petroleum Company (NNPC) on the Ubeta gas field, which is expected to supply gas to Nigeria LNG’s Train 7 project. He also referenced the more recent IMA project as part of continued investment activity.
In Lagos, the Omi Eko project is expected to transform water transportation by introducing 75 electric ferries, 25 upgraded terminals, and 15 routes covering 140 kilometres of waterways. The project is receiving support from France, through the French Development Agency (AFD), alongside the European Union and the European Investment Bank.
Niarfeix also highlighted the Lekki Deep Sea Port, where CMA CGM has agreed to operate the container terminal. The port has a 14-metre draft and an annual handling capacity of 2.5 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), positioning it as a significant logistics asset for international trade.
Beyond attracting French investment into Nigeria, he said the chamber is working to facilitate Nigerian businesses’ access to the French market.
Niarfeix said the FNCCI had extended its activities beyond Lagos through its first Executive Paris Leadership Training Programme and Business Mission earlier this year. The initiative connected Nigerian executives with French investors, institutions and policymakers.
Favier said Nigerian financial institutions are also strengthening their presence in France. With Access Bank opening a French Desk in Paris, major Nigerian banks, including Zenith Bank, United Bank for Africa and First Bank of Nigeria, have established a presence in the country.
Further noting that major investment opportunities are also emerging in agribusiness and technology; he said Nigerian companies, JR Farms and Babafood have established operations in France via coffee production and exports, animal feed, cassava processing and the import-export of agro-industrial products. He further revealed that Flour Mills of Nigeria Group has also expressed interest in developing its presence in the French market.
To support this expansion, he said Nigeria participated in the International Agriculture Show in France in 2026, marking its second appearance at the event after the 2024 edition.
“In technology, GecX60, an Internet of Things start-up, has established a research and development centre within the Orange Group incubator in Blagnac, France. Convexity, a consultancy specialising in blockchain and payment solutions for non-governmental organisations, is also preparing to establish its first European office in Paris,” Favier said.
To deepen cooperation in agriculture, both countries have established the Franco-Nigerian Agri-Business Club, a platform designed to promote collaboration across the agrifood value chain.
The initiative, he said, is expected to encourage French agribusiness investors to support local capacity building, agricultural mechanisation and agro-processing, while helping reduce post-harvest losses and create opportunities for growth in Nigeria’s agricultural sector.
Niarfeix commended the Federal Government for its ongoing reforms and efforts to improve the ease of doing business, saying the measures are providing a firmer foundation for local and foreign investment.
He said French companies increasingly regard Nigeria as a strategic economic partner rather than simply a market for their products and services.
The French Week is expected to showcase existing investments, strengthen business-to-business engagement, and identify new areas for commercial cooperation between the two countries.

articles.title: India-EU investment protection agreement under discussion: Goyal - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: India-EU investment protection agreement under discussion: Goyal  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
India and the European Union are actively negotiating an Investment Protection Agreement to foster economic ties. The introduction of necessary legal changes for the Geographical Indications pact is set for Parliament's agenda.
                                    
                    
                    
                    
                                        Investment Protection Agreement (IPA) between India and the European Union are underway, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has said.
He also said some legal changes are required for an agreement on Geographical Indications (GIs) with the EU, which the ministry is going to introduce in Parliament. "Discussions are underway on a bilateral investment agreement or the IPA, and for the GI pact, we need to make some legal changes," he told reporters here.
India and the 27-nation European Union announced the conclusion of negotiations for a free trade agreement on January 27, which is touted as "mother of all deals". The EU is already a leading investor in India. About 6,000 European firms are present in India.
A GI is primarily an agricultural, natural or manufactured product (handicrafts and industrial goods) originating from a definite geographical territory. An IPA provides a framework to protect investments made by companies and investors in another country.It aims to ensure fair and non-discriminatory treatment, protect investors against unlawful expropriation and provide mechanisms for resolving investment-related disputes.
Such agreements help boost investor confidence, reduce policy-related risks and encourage cross-border investment by offering greater certainty and transparency in the host country's regulatory framework. Similarly, a GI agreement between India and the European Union would protect region-specific products in each other's markets, helping prevent imitation and misuse of their names.
Goyal said that these pacts would come into force after the implementation of the free trade agreement, which is likely to be signed in December and may come into force next in March or April.
He added that India's young and talented population, growing middle class, fast-growing economy and rapid adoption of modern technology make it an attractive investment destination. With preferential access to economies accounting for 76 per cent of global GDP, India's trade opportunities would increase significantly, he added.

articles.title: Russia and Ukraine begin local ceasefire in frontline city - Financial Times
articles.summary: Russia and Ukraine begin local ceasefire in frontline city  Financial TimesCeasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say  BBCOleshky truce appears to hold as two European leaders have ‘frank’ call with Putin  The GuardianUkrainian refugees will be sent to Russia under Melania Trump’s ceasefire  The TelegraphFirst lady Melania Trump says Ukraine-Russia ceasefire expanded within Kherson  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Simply sign up to the War in Ukraine myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox.
Russia and Ukraine began a localised ceasefire in southern Ukraine overnight under a US-backed agreement to evacuate civilians trapped in the Russian-occupied frontline city of Oleshky.
Russian forces will start clearing mines off the roads leading to the embattled city, where about 2,000 people have been caught in crossfire between the two armies and face severe food shortages.
Buses should take people out of Oleshky on Thursday morning, while humanitarian aid will be brought in for residents who decline to leave.
The ceasefire, which will last until November 1, is “the most significant de-escalation since 2022”, one of Ukraine’s chief negotiators, David Arakhamia, wrote on social media.
Arakhamia and the White House said first lady Melania Trump helped secure the agreement, which was announced on October 23 after weeks of campaigning by Kyiv. Pope Leo XIV had called Russian President Vladimir Putin on October 16 to push for the ceasefire.
Melania Trump said on Tuesday the ceasefire had been “expanded” to the entire Kherson region.
Ukrainian authorities had said on Monday that the ceasefire would apply to the Kherson region as a whole and confirmed that both sides were adhering to it on Tuesday afternoon.
The deal came during a push to renew peace talks to end the conflict in Ukraine. US President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff met Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo last week before travelling to St Petersburg for talks with Putin.
Putin on Tuesday held a phone call with the leaders of Norway and Finland, who hosted the Oslo talks and called on the Russian leader to end the war. Ukraine and Russia have agreed to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi in coming days.
Oleshky, a quiet city on the Dnipro River with a population of about 24,000 before Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, has been cut off from the rest of the region by drone strikes and mines, making it nearly impossible for food and medicine to reach it. Most of the city does not have electricity, heating or water.
Residents “are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, preserves and even snails”, Ukrainian foreign minister Andriy Sybiha wrote on X this month.
People who agreed to leave would be taken to Crimea or Russia before they were able to return to Ukraine, people with knowledge of the discussions told the FT.
“Russia will do everything it can to de-mine in such a way that these people go towards Russia and remain there,” Zelenskyy warned in an interview on Ukrainian television on Sunday. “Our people and society need to be prepared for how they will sell it: ‘Look, we see thousands of people who really want to go to Russia, and those fascists were shelling them.’”
Zelenskyy accused Russia of blocking and mining the road out of Oleshky, while Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has alleged that Ukrainian forces had hindered deliveries of food and medicine.
Ukrainian forces have increasingly targeted Russian supply lines in southern Ukraine in what then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov called a “logistics lockdown” in May. The intensified drone strikes aimed to cut off Crimea and weaken Russian frontline units.
Moscow took control of Oleshky in the early days of the invasion, and the city turned into a frontline position following the Russian retreat in autumn 2022. The Russian destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in 2023 triggered a massive flood that devastated the city and probably killed hundreds of residents, an Associated Press investigation found.
One local, who fled the city in 2023, said residents had told him the situation turned critical a year ago, as it became increasingly deadly for people to drive out of the city. A humanitarian volunteer, who had been helping people flee, died in January when his vehicle hit a mine hidden by snow.
By summer this year, drone footage of the thoroughfare heading out of Oleshky showed a road littered with charred vehicles.
Russian drone units on the Dnipro have repeatedly hit civilians, including ambulances and pedestrians, in nearby Kherson and other settlements. A UN commission concluded last year the attacks “suggest a co-ordinated state policy, on the part of the Russian authorities, to force the population of Kherson Province to leave the area”. The commission said the attacks “amount to crimes against humanity”.
Localised ceasefires have been rare and fraught with tension since 2022. A corridor in the Zaporizhzhia region allowed civilians to cross the frontline during the first months of the full-scale invasion but was closed after a Russian missile strike on a civilian convoy killed 32 people in September 2022.
Several localised ceasefires have been brokered by the International Atomic Energy Agency to repair infrastructure serving the Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant.
Separately, a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv killed one person and injured 15 overnight, Ukraine’s state emergency service reported on Tuesday. Missiles damaged a university building, a metro station and a bridge in the capital.

articles.title: Captured Russians say there is one place on Kupiansk front they will not go: "Orion" safety corridor - Euromaidan Press
articles.summary: Captured Russians say there is one place on Kupiansk front they will not go: "Orion" safety corridor  Euromaidan PressUkraine is arming war robots with grenade launchers to hit the Russians so its soldiers don't have to get too close  Business Insider"Death Strip": "Orion" ground robots carried out nearly 100% successful missions near Kupiansk  LIGA.netUkraine Uses Robot Dogs to Deliver Explosives, Officer Says  Военное дело
articles.full_text:
Captured Russian soldiers have a rule for one stretch of the Kupiansk front: go anywhere, but not there.
That stretch is the “safety corridor” the “Orion” unit of Ukraine’s Offensive Guard brigade “Pomsta” says it has built for its ground robots. The zone is so lethal that, by the unit’s count, 88% of attacking Russians are killed before they reach their positions, and Russian armor cannot get within 25 kilometers, the military outlet ArmyInform reports.
Behind that shield, the unit says its ground robots have run dozens of fully autonomous missions through the most dangerous ground on the axis, with a success rate of 99.57%. The results made Orion the top-ranked unit for effectiveness on the South-Kupiansk axis in September within Ukraine’s battlefield management system, DELTA.
“You can go anywhere, just not into the Orion zone”
The claim that the Russians now avoid the sector, the unit says, comes from them themselves.
“Prisoners admit in interviews: 'You can go anywhere, just not into the Orion zone.' Eighty-eight percent of the enemy is destroyed before reaching their positions, and Russian equipment cannot approach closer than 25 kilometers,” the unit says.
That is what opens the corridor. Where a human supply run would be a death sentence, a robot can cross, and cross again.
The quiet blood of the front
The point, the unit says, is to take the soldier out of the deadliest job on the front: carrying ammunition and the wounded across open fire.
“We broke the stereotype that supplying the army takes truck convoys and hundreds of soldiers under targeted fire. Our robotic systems are the ‘quiet blood’ of the front,” Vladyslav Zolotarov, an officer in the unit’s staff control group, says.
When Russia thinks our positions are depleted, a tracked platform quietly comes in at night and brings in a ton of ammunition.
In September alone, the unit says, its wheeled and tracked robots ran 85 of the hardest combat missions and hauled more than 30,000 kilograms of cargo. Its evacuation record is the line it is proudest of: four missions pulling wounded soldiers out by robot, all four successful, not one man lost.
Ukraine has bet heavily on this kind of machine, aiming to field 50,000 ground robots to keep its troops out of the drone-ruled kill zone.

Gold Holds Near $4000 as Fed Meeting Begins
Spot gold is edging lower early Tuesday ahead of the start of the Federal Reserve’s two-day policy meeting. Traders are blaming a stronger dollar for today’s weakness.
Prices fell below the psychological $4000 level for the first time since mid-to-late July last week. However, prices have been consolidating since then as traders absorbed the steep plunge. Last week’s 4% loss marked the biggest decline since June. The catalyst behind the steep loss was a surge in oil prices to a multi-month high. The move in energy led to increased inflation concerns while reinforcing U.S. rate hike expectations.
December Rate-Hike Odds Hold the Real Risk
Currently, Fed Funds traders don’t expect a rate hike on Wednesday, but they are looking for the Fed to hike rates at least a quarter point in December. Gold traders are not too worried about the outcome of this meeting, but rather what the central bankers offer in terms of fresh guidance on the outlook for interest rates.
With the October FedWatch Tool showing an 89.5% probability that the Fed holds rates at 3.75% to 4.00%, the risk is to the downside for gold. articles.summary: South Korean Defense Groups Shift to European Production  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On

South Korean defense groups are moving production into European plants
EU funding rules reward local content, control and design authority
Local lines mature around 2030, as SAFE lending closes
Europe’s military spending increased by 14% in 2025 to $864 billion, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute and some of that demand that would have been hard to predict a decade ago ended up in the Changwon assembly lines. South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration recorded exports of $15.4 billion for the same year, with Poland accounting for more than 40% of the total. South Korean defense groups gained this position because they were delivering tanks and self-propelled guns at a time when European production lines were carrying years of backlogs. The advantage of speed is waning as Brussels ties the new common funds to European content and European control. For Hanwha Aerospace and Hyundai Rotem, the question now shifts to how much industry they are willing to install on European soil and whether their finances will hold up when the current boom in orders weakens.
Readiness 2030, SAFE and EDIP Rewrite the Rules for Non-EU Suppliers
The White Paper on European Defence, known as Readiness 2030, was presented by the European Commission in March 2025 together with the ReArm Europe plan, which aims to mobilise up to €800 billion. Most of this amount comes from the activation of the national escape clause of the Stability and Growth Pact, i.e. from national budgets that gain fiscal space. The second strand is SAFE, a €150 billion loan instrument established by Council Regulation 2025/1106 on 27 May 2025. Poland received the highest allocation, €43.7 billion and Romania the second, €16.68 billion, with the Romanian loan agreement signed on May 12, 2026, i.e. these are the two markets where Korean companies have invested the most. The third tool is the European Defence Industry Programme, the EDIP, established by Regulation 2025/2643 in December 2025 with a budget of €1.5 billion, of which over €700 million is directed, according to the work programme adopted by the Commission on 30 March 2026, to increasing European production.
Article 16 of SAFE stipulates that contractors and subcontractors must be established in the Union, in an EEA EFTA State or in Ukraine, have their executive management there and not be controlled by a third country, with the possibility of derogation where the entity has passed a foreign direct investment screening or when the State of establishment confirms security guarantees. The often misinterpreted threshold of 35% does not refer to the contract value. It measures the cost of components sourced from outside the eligible territories as a percentage of the estimated cost of the final product components, which makes the origin of the fire control system or power unit much more important than the place of final assembly. The regulation allows bilateral agreements with countries that have a Security and Defence Partnership with the Union and Canada became the first non-European country to secure such an agreement, with Member States’ endorsement in December 2025. South Korea signed its own Partnership in November 2024, however the EU-Korea summit in Brussels in June 2026 resulted in the opening of negotiations on a classified information security agreement rather than participation in SAFE.
The EDIP also explicitly sets out a design authority requirement. Beyond the corresponding 35% threshold in Article 10, the beneficiary must be able to modify the product and replace components throughout its lifecycle without a third-country veto, with the possibility of a legally binding commitment to full autonomy by 31 December 2033. National procurement with national funds is left out of both regimes, so the image of a Europe that collectively excludes Korean weapons is inaccurate. A K9 that Warsaw buys with its own money is not judged by the rules of SAFE, while the same K9, if financed by a SAFE loan, must pass the criteria of origin and control and if it claims support from the EDIP it must also prove that Seoul does not hold a key in its design. The three channels are not interchangeable and this explains why local production has become a matter of access to specific sources of financing for Korean groups.
Hanwha Aerospace Moves Production to Romania and Poland
Romania signed a contract with Hanwha Aerospace in July 2024 for 54 K9 self-propelled guns and 36 K10 ammunition resupply vehicles, thus becoming the sixth NATO member state to use the K9. Nineteen months later, on February 12, 2026, the subsidiary Hanwha Aerospace Romania, founded in 2025 as a Romanian company, laid the foundation stone of the Hanwha Armoured Vehicle Centre of Excellence Europe in Petrești, Dâmbovița County. The facility will cover approximately 181,055 square meters, with assembly lines, test facilities, a 1,751-meter driving track and research and development laboratories. The company presents it as its first production base in Europe, initially focused on assembly, integration, testing, and lifecycle support for the K9 and K10, to localize up to 80% through Romanian industry. According to the company, cooperation with more than 30 Romanian partners has already begun.
In Poland the format is different. On September 3, 2025, the first day of the MSPO exhibition in Kielce, Hanwha Aerospace and the Polish group WB Group signed an agreement for a joint venture that will locally produce the CGR-080 guided missile, with a range of about 80 kilometers, for the Polish army’s Homar-K multiple launcher system. The agreement provides for a gradual transfer of technology, about 250 positions of specialized personnel and serial production that will reach an advanced stage before the end of 2028. Four months later, on December 29, 2025, the Polish Armaments Agency signed an executive contract worth about 14 billion zlotys, close to $4 billion, with a consortium led by the Hanwha WB Advanced System joint venture. The missiles will be manufactured in a special unit within Poland and deliveries will begin in 2030.
The two schemes share a logic that goes beyond assembly. Ammunition is being consumed and a guided missile factory in Poland is securing revenue for as long as the Polish military is training and replenishing stockpiles, while a lifecycle center in Romania is turning maintenance, upgrades and spare parts into local infrastructure, which a competitor would struggle to displace after a decade of operation with Romanian personnel and Romanian suppliers. One detail in the text of the Polish agreement stands out, as the roadmap for new types of missiles will be drafted in accordance with both Polish defense procurement rules and the Republic of Korea’s export control regime. The joint venture has a Polish base and a Polish co-owner; the relevant announcements did not disclose each side's percentage of participation and the technology transfer continues to follow licenses issued in Seoul.
Hyundai Rotem’s K2PL Localizes Assembly but Keeps Design Control in Korea
Hyundai Rotem took a different route in the same country. The framework agreement approved in Warsaw on July 27, 2022 concerns a total of 1,000 K2 tanks and their Polonised version, the K2PL, along with support vehicles, training and technology transfer. The first executive contract of August 2022, with a net value of $3.37 billion, covered 180 K2 tanks made in Korea and the last batch of 20 tanks arrived in Poland on November 13, 2025. The second contract, signed on August 1, 2025 at the Bumar-Łabędy plant in Gliwice, is valued at around $6.5 billion and provides for another 180 tanks. Of these, 116 in the K2GF configuration are delivered from 2026 to 2027 and 64 in the K2PL configuration from 2028 to 2030, with the first three K2PLs being built in Korea for testing and the remaining 61 in Gliwice. The contract also includes 31 armoured recovery vehicles, 25 engineering vehicles and 25 bridge-laying vehicles, with delivery from 2029 to 2031.
The technology transfer outlined by the Polish Ministry of National Defense for the second contract is specific and delimited: the possibility of final assembly in Polish companies and the ability to fully maintain and operate the tanks. Hyundai Rotem undertakes to equip Bumar-Łabędy with tools and machinery for the K2PL line and the accompanying vehicles. On April 27, 2026, the two companies signed the agreement regulating production, with Bumar-Łabędy assembling 61 K2PL tanks and 72 support vehicles as a subcontractor, while Hyundai Rotem remains the main contractor of the program and with the first K2PL coming off the Gliwice line in 2028. In relation to the K2GF, the K2PL acquires an active vehicle protection system, a drone-countering system and additional armor, while it will be able to use programmable ammunition of other origins and a Polish 12.7mm heavy machine gun.
The comparison with Hanwha Aerospace is mainly about who raises the capital and who holds the control. Hanwha Aerospace invests in its own European entities, a Romanian subsidiary and a Polish joint venture, taking on the risk of facilities that need to be filled with orders. Hyundai Rotem installs a line in a Polish state-owned company of the PGZ group and retains the position of main contractor and designer, with much less exposure to fixed assets. The second model fits more easily into the establishment and control criterion of Article 16, since the manufacturer is Polish, but leaves open the origin of the components and the design authority, which remain largely Korean. The leadership of the Polish Ministry of National Defense has stated that it wants K2PL to become an export success for Łabędy, an ambition that presupposes an agreement on who has the right to sell to third parties a tank designed in Korea and assembled in Silesia.

articles.title: Plan for multibillion-pound Sizewell nuclear plant a ‘terrible deal’ for UK taxpayers, MPs say - The Guardian
articles.summary: Plan for multibillion-pound Sizewell nuclear plant a ‘terrible deal’ for UK taxpayers, MPs say  The GuardianSizewell nuclear plant is ‘terrible deal’ for British taxpayers, MPs conclude  Financial TimesNIA responds to the PAC report  Nuclear Industry AssociationMPs call Sizewell C financing a ‘terrible deal’  Construction NewsSizewell C investors set to cash in and leave taxpayers to foot the bill, PAC warns  UK Parliament
articles.full_text:
The government’s plan to fund a multibillion-pound nuclear plant at the Sizewell site in Suffolk represents a “terrible deal” for the UK taxpayer over the rest of the century, according to the government’s spending watchdog.
MPs on the public accounts committee (PAC) have warned the government that the cost of the Sizewell C nuclear reactor could spiral to almost £48bn, leaving bill payers on the hook to provide an extra £9.8bn to construct the plant before 2040 and a further £12bn over its 60-year operating life.
Taxpayers and consumers face a “high level of risk”, according to PAC, after the government agreed to take a near-45% stake in the nuclear plant, which is considered a successor project to the heavily delayed Hinkley Point C nuclear plant in Somerset.
Under the terms of the multibillion-pound deal, which will be paid for through taxes and energy bills, the UK government holds a 44.9% stake while French state nuclear developer EDF has a 12.5% stake.
The rest of the funding has come from private investors including the British Gas owner Centrica, which holds a 15% share, alongside the Canadian investment group La Caisse, which holds 20%, and the investment manager Amber Infrastructure, which has a7.6% stake.
The UK government was forced to take a larger than expected share of the project after buying out Chinese state nuclear developer CGN, which had been allowed to hold a 20% stake in Sizewell C before national security concerns emerged.
The watchdog warned that while the British public could be called on to shoulder multibillion-pound cost overruns, the nuclear project’s private investors would only need to put in an extra £30m.
Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the PAC chair, said: “The high level of risk borne by taxpayers and consumers for the construction of Sizewell C is extraordinary. Private investors look set for significant returns on their investments, while customers are likely to be saddled with higher energy bills.”
He urged the government to “focus on the successful delivery of this project”, and in building confidence in the UK’s nuclear industry more broadly, so that taxpayers will “never be put in this position again”.
A government spokesperson said the report “completely ignores that investors are incentivised to complete construction as cheaply and quickly as possible” through the terms of the deal.
“Once operational, Sizewell C could save £2bn a year across the energy system, cutting costs for families up and down the country, and the project is already making good progress with over 2,000 workers on site,” the spokesperson added.
The government expects Sizewell C to cost between £40.5bn and £47.7bn and to complete construction between 2039 and 2043. The committee has called on the government to provide the scenario analysis it used to underpin its cost estimates for the project within the next three months. It also asked ministers to provide an update on the project’s development every six months to keep track of its progress.
Critics of the project, including Alison Downes of the Stop Sizewell C campaign group and Prof Steve Thomas of Greenwich Business School, who provided joint evidence to the committee, have suggested that the cost of abandoning the project today would be lower than the cost of paying inflated energy bills over 60 years “multiple times over”.
They called on the government to rule out using this funding model for future nuclear projects. “All it offers is a free ride for investors and financial pain for households,” they said in a joint statement.
Tom Greatrex, the chief executive of the Nuclear Industry Association, said Sizewell C would provide “clean, reliable and constantly available power” that could save households billions from paying the cost of balancing the grid or building extra network connections.
“Currently, the consumer is footing a bill of £2.8bn so far this year to manage a dysfunctional grid, paying both for wind to stop generating at some times, and for gas-powered backup at others,” he said.

articles.title: China's Stock Market Has Lost $2.4 Trillion as Investors Doubt Its AI Boom Will Ever Pay Off - Decrypt
articles.summary: China's Stock Market Has Lost $2.4 Trillion as Investors Doubt Its AI Boom Will Ever Pay Off  DecryptIn China, the AI bubble has already burst  ReutersChinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll  The GuardianChina Steps In to Rescue Stocks, But the Market Continues to Fall  The New York TimesChina AI Hardware Firms Face Earnings Test After Stock Selloff  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
In brief
- Stocks on China's mainland have lost about $2.4 trillion in market value since May, and the STAR 50 index of tech and chip companies is down 40% in under four months.
- AI companies make up 42% of the market value of Chinese shares and 57% of trading, per Goldman Sachs, while U.S. curbs now target Chinese robots and data center parts.
- Brent crude above $111 and 10-year Treasury yields near 5% are pressuring risk assets worldwide, with Bitcoin briefly under $80,000 ahead of the Fed's October 28 decision.
Stocks on China's mainland have lost about $2.4 trillion in market value, the total worth of all their shares, since May, as investors lose faith that Beijing's AI boom will ever turn a profit.
That is more than South Korea's entire economy produces in a year.
AI companies now make up 42% of the market value of Chinese shares listed on the mainland and in Hong Kong, and 57% of trading, according to Goldman Sachs. So when AI stocks fall, the whole market falls with them.
The CSI 300, an index of China's 300 biggest listed companies, entered a bear market on October 22, meaning a drop of at least 20% from its peak.
The sharpest damage hit Shanghai's STAR 50, an index of 50 large tech and chip companies. It fell 40% in less than four months, erasing about $480 billion.
It still trades at roughly 100 times earnings, a ratio that shows how many years of current profit investors are paying for, down from nearly 250 at its peak. The Nasdaq 100, the U.S. tech benchmark, sits around 30.
DeepSeek, a Chinese startup, released a cheap and powerful chatbot in January 2025, and Nvidia, the U.S. company whose chips power most AI, lost nearly $600 billion in market value in a single day. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, also produced by a Chinese AI lab, sent chip stocks tumbling again in July.
Beijing then pushed its tech giants toward homegrown chips: According to the Financial Times, its internet regulator reportedly told companies including ByteDance and Alibaba to stop buying Nvidia chips in September 2025. Z.ai, a Beijing lab, says it trained its GLM-5.2 model entirely on Huawei chips.
Analysts blame weak spending by Chinese consumers and doubts that AI companies can earn back what they have invested. Robot maker Unitree drew retail orders for 8,000 times the shares on offer when it listed in August, and its stock has since lost almost half its value since launch even after a significant recovery this week.
Shares of Chinese robot maker Unitree Robotics have jumped more than 60% since Oct. 15, lifting its market value to 271.8 billion yuan (roughly $40.8 billion). Investors are betting that smarter AI will give its robots the brains they lack. The wager is that the technology behind chatbots can soon operate machines in the physical world, a field called physical AI. If it can, a robot that tidies a room or folds laundry on command stops being a lab demo, and the companies that build the bodies, m...
“The stock market later evolved into a speculative crazy bull,” said Dong Baozhen, a Beijing-based fund manager. “And now we see the bubble bursting.”
The U.S. Federal Communications Commission banned imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots in July on national security grounds. Washington is also moving to ban Chinese-made optical parts from U.S. data centers, and the makers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink are down about 60% from their peaks.

articles.title: Failure to ratify the EU trade deal would cost Australia far more than beef - The Conversation
articles.summary: Failure to ratify the EU trade deal would cost Australia far more than beef  The Conversation
articles.full_text:
Australia and the European Union agreed on a comprehensive free-trade agreement (FTA) in March, after nearly eight years negotiating and much political rancour.
The agreement abolishes almost all bilateral tariffs, covering 98% of Australian goods exports and broadens our export base at a time of high US tariffs.
Seven months on, the fight has moved to Canberra. Although the government signed the treaty, parliament must pass the laws required to give it effect, such as changing tariff schedules.
Passage through the lower house is certain. In the Senate, however, Labor holds 30 of 76 Senate seats and needs nine extra Senate votes, from a mix of Coalition, Greens, One Nation, and cross-bench senators.
The Coalition is split
With 27 Senate seats, the Coalition’s position matters most, but it is split.
In mid-October Nationals Senate leader Matt Canavan and Nationals frontbencher Bridget McKenzie said the Coalition would oppose the deal, citing insufficient gains in beef, lamb and dairy.
Liberals quickly contradicted them, though some share concerns about the agreement’s commitments on climate and labour rights to meet the International Labour Organization’s rules.
Those concerns are overstated. The Paris Agreement climate? commitments are voluntary and can be revised, while the deal requires no new International Labour Organization ratifications.
If Liberal leader Angus Taylor sides with the Nationals, Labor would need the Greens’ ten senators. However, under new leader David Shoebridge, the Greens may seek to drive harder bargains in legislative negotiations with the government.
The alternative — all four One Nation senators, combined with all five independent senators — seems unlikely.
Why not renegotiate the deal?
Some have suggested the deal should be renegotiated to achieve even greater market access.
Could we go back for more? No. European Commission spokesperson Olof Gill told Politico last week:
Once negotiations are done, they are done.
Farrell shows farmers the beef
Trade Minister Don Farrell told ABC Radio National the beef industry wanted A$3 billion in new trade and he got them $2 billion. He said “the rest of the Australian economy” should not be penalised because of that.
While still well short of sales to China, Japan or the US, the deal sharply lifts Australia’s dedicated quota from 4,400 tonnes to 35,000 tonnes once phased in, with the current 20% tariff scrapped from day one.
In 2019, during the first Trump administration, Europe handed the United States a dedicated 35,000-tonne share of the grain-fed beef quota. This came at the expense of non-US suppliers, including Australia. Successive Coalition and Labor governments have tried to claw back Australia’s share.
Farrell argued that one sector’s disappointment should not deny opportunities to everyone else:
My job is to represent the national interest, not just one section of the Australian economy.
That is the judgement governments must make. Trade negotiations involve compromise. Neither side gets everything it wants.
Australia’s trade agreements have often attracted criticism, but implementation has generally had bipartisan support.
Critical minerals have been overlooked
The focus on agricultural exports also overlooks many other opportunities, notably critical minerals — the materials needed for batteries, wind turbines, electric vehicles and defence equipment.
The International Energy Agency identifies financing and supply-chain concentration as major challenges. China’s dominance in refining makes developing alternatives difficult.
Australia has substantial resources of critical minerals. What we lack are buyers, lenders and capital. Mine developers need long-term purchase contracts, known as offtake agreements, which help convince financiers a project will generate reliable income.
Europe’s Critical Raw Materials Act says by 2030 no more than 65% of any strategic mineral should come from a single country. The FTA supports cooperation on mining, processing and investment. It gives European businesses greater confidence to commit to Australian projects.
Arafura’s Nolans rare earths project near Alice Springs illustrates the opportunity. Government agency Austrade reports an A$84 million investment from Germany’s state development bank KfW and a long-term supply agreement with turbine manufacturer Siemens Gamesa.
Nolans is designed to combine mining and processing on site. That is the onshore processing every Australian politician says they want. The Minerals Council recently backed the EU deal for that reason.
These arrangements show how European customers and financing can support Australia’s mining sector. The trade deal with the EU unlocks more of these opportunities.
Remember the rules-based order?
Recent experience — ever since US President Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs —demonstrates that allies are not protected from US trade barriers. Nor can we forget China’s use of economic pressure against Australian exporters of wine, barley and lobster.
Australia is wedged between a protectionist ally and a coercive customer.
The answer is not to abandon either relationship. Rather, it is to build more options. Europe’s market of about 450 million people, investment capacity, and closer security relationship with Australia make it an important partner that, like Australia, still believes in rules.
Ratification is now or never
Europe’s window will not stay open for ever. Ratification needs a “qualified majority” of EU governments, or at least 15 of 27 countries holding 65% of the population.
Politico is calling the year ahead a perfect political storm. A succession of national elections clouds the horizon with Spain on November 29, France and Italy in 2027, while Germany’s coalition is under serious strain from far-right challengers.
Failure to ratify now, on either side, would confront much more challenging political dynamics in Europe and Australia. It is this deal or none.
The Coalition started this in 2018 because it was the right call. It still is. Let’s not allow the perfect to get in the way of the good.

articles.title: A strategic role reversal: how China’s EV tech and Asean ties reshape Sino-European trade - The Standard (HK)
articles.summary: A strategic role reversal: how China’s EV tech and Asean ties reshape Sino-European trade  The Standard (HK)
articles.full_text:
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier’s visit to China notably began at the Volkswagen Group China Technology Company in Hefei. Ahead of the tour, the Chinese-German joint venture FAW-Volkswagen launched Jetta’s new M6 model, marking the German automotive industry’s latest attempt to penetrate China’s hyper-competitive electric vehicle market.
Equipped with Chinese lithium batteries, intelligent driving chips, and AI services, the M6 embodies a fundamental paradigm shift. The outdated model of “German technology, assembled in China” has squarely been replaced by “Chinese digital architecture built around legacy German mechanical engineering.”
As China leaps from exporting lower-level consumer goods to advanced manufacturing, it inevitably threatens Germany’s once-dominant automotive industry. This evolution has triggered a chronic wrestling match between China and the European Union over ballooning trade imbalances.
Consequently, Brussels has proposed a series of trade barriers. Beyond punitive tariffs on Chinese hybrid and electric vehicles, the EU is set to impose a 2 euro (HK$17.5) processing fee on foreign e-commerce parcels starting November 1. Furthermore, early 2027 will see new trade defense measures targeting Chinese chemicals, furniture, and machinery.
Navigating the de-risking era
Yet, Steinmeier’s visit underscores that in the renewable energy sector, the two economies remain highly complementary. Europe urgently needs affordable Chinese green tech to alleviate inflation exacerbated by global oil shocks from the US-initiated conflict with Iran, while China requires the vast European consumer market to absorb its industrial output.
Tellingly, at the exact same time, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is visiting Singapore, South Korea, and Japan. This highest-level “synchronized diplomacy” executes Berlin’s “de-risking” policy: maintaining economic ties with Beijing while strengthening Indo-Pacific alliances. Encouragingly, it demonstrates Germany’s determination to maintain strategic autonomy, refusing a Washington-led “hard decoupling” as the transatlantic rift under Donald Trump widens.
In Singapore, Chancellor Merz is pushing for deeper collaboration on open market access within Asean. Paradoxically, this provides a vital lifeline for China’s global supply chain restructuring. As Chinese firms aggressively offshore manufacturing to Southeast Asia under the “China Plus One” strategy, an open EU-Asean trade corridor allows them to supply intermediate goods to Asean factories.
These factories then export finished products to Europe, bypassing direct EU-China tariffs. Ultimately, a robust economic circulation between China, Asean, and the EU helps Beijing navigate this new era of global protectionism.
Echoes of historic cooperation
As two of the world’s largest economic blocs, China and the EU cannot afford a complete decoupling. Trade imbalances must be addressed, but they should not choke off vital economic cooperation.
This sentiment was echoed during Steinmeier’s specially arranged visit to the former Hefei residence of Li Hongzhang. As a pioneer of late-Qing China’s push for an industrial revolution, Li – often dubbed the “Bismarck of the East” – visited Germany in 1896 to meet Otto von Bismarck and learn from German industrial advancement.
Today, 130 years later, at the dawn of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, the tables have turned. Germany now urgently needs Chinese digital infrastructure and battery prowess to achieve its own industrial restructuring. History repeatedly demonstrates that China and Germany have far more to gain from cooperation than conflict.

Brazil’s Pulp Trade Faces US Tariffs and EU Deforestation Rules
|  | 
Brazil’s pulp industry faces mounting trade pressures as US tariffs affect selected pulp grades, new US trade-duty proceedings target high-purity dissolving pulp, and the European Union prepares to apply its deforestation regulation. The challenges come as Brazilian pulp exports declined in the first half of 2026.
According to the Brazilian Tree Industry Association (Ibá), Brazil exported approximately 9.4 million tonnes of pulp in the first half of 2026, down 10.5% year on year from around 10.5 million tonnes in the same period of 2025. Export revenue fell 4% to approximately US$5.2 billion, while domestic production remained practically stable at 13.9 million tonnes.
Ibá attributed the broader cultivated-tree sector’s export decline to increased protectionism and disruptions to global supply chains. The sector’s total exports, including pulp, paper and wood panels, reached US$7.5 billion during the period, down 5.9% year on year.
US trade measures target dissolving pulp
The United States introduced an additional 25% Section 301 tariff on specified Brazilian goods, effective July 22, 2026. Most wood pulp products were exempted from the additional tariff, but high-purity dissolving pulp was excluded from the exemptions. Consequently, the measure does not affect all Brazilian pulp grades equally.
Separately, on October 13, the US Department of Commerce announced final affirmative determinations in anti-dumping investigations into high-purity dissolving pulp from Brazil and Norway, as well as a countervailing duty investigation into Brazilian imports.
For Brazil, Commerce calculated an estimated weighted-average dumping margin of 6.50% and an adjusted anti-dumping cash-deposit rate of 6.40%. It also determined a subsidy rate of 9.37% for Brazilian imports covered by the countervailing duty investigation.
Bracell Bahia Specialty Cellulose S.A. and Bracell SP Celulose Ltda. were treated as a single entity for the anti-dumping determination. For the countervailing duty investigation, Commerce identified Bracell Bahia Specialty Cellulose S.A. and its cross-owned companies, Bracell Bahia Florestal Ltda., Bracell SP Celulose Limitada and Bracell SP Florestal Ltda.
The determinations do not, by themselves, conclude the proceedings. The US International Trade Commission (ITC) must make the corresponding injury determination. If the ITC finds no material injury or threat of material injury to the US industry, the proceedings will be terminated and cash deposits refunded. If the injury determination is affirmative, Commerce can proceed with issuing duty orders.
EU deforestation rules approach implementation
The European Union’s Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) is scheduled to begin applying to large and medium-sized operators on December 30, 2026. Most micro and small operators have until June 30, 2027, while certain micro and small operators already covered by the EU Timber Regulation face the earlier date.
The regulation covers wood and specified wood-derived products, subject to its product scope and applicable requirements. Companies placing covered products on the EU market must meet the relevant deforestation-free, legality and due-diligence obligations.
For Brazilian pulp producers exporting to Europe, compliance will require appropriate supply-chain traceability and documentation demonstrating that covered products meet the regulation’s requirements. Europe is an important destination for Brazilian pulp, making the implementation timetable commercially relevant for exporters.
With lower first-half export volumes, US trade measures affecting selected products and the EUDR’s application date approaching, Brazilian pulp producers face a changing regulatory and commercial environment. articles.title: EU seeks to expand trade ties with Asia amid rising barriers - Operativ Məlumat Mərkəzi

articles.full_text:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said during a visit to Singapore on October 27 that the European Union was seeking to deepen trade ties with Asia. Merz said rising global trade barriers posed a threat to international trade, AnewZ reports.
Merz called for closer cooperation with Southeast Asian economies and members of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), which includes 12 countries. He defended open markets and predictable trade rules in response to growing protectionism.
A study published in July by the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) found that global trade policy activity in the first five months of 2026 was almost twice as high as in the same period of 2024. The increase was driven mainly by restrictive measures.
Why is Europe strengthening economic ties with Asia?
Strengthening economic ties with Asia could help Europe diversify its export markets and investment partnerships amid uncertainty over US tariffs and Chinese trade restrictions.
“In an international environment once again shaped by competition among major powers, we must defend our interests,” Merz said.
Speaking alongside Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, Merz said the European Union, with about 450 million consumers, wanted to strengthen partnerships based on open competition, reliability and rules-based trade.
“This is a deliberate response to what we are seeing today ... We want to do things differently and show that there is a better way,” Merz said.
He also called for stronger ties with CPTPP members. The agreement includes Japan, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, Mexico, Singapore and Malaysia. The United States and China are not members.
Trade between the European Union and ASEAN
According to the European Commission, trade in goods between the European Union and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) reached 274.9 billion euros (about $319 billion) in 2025, making ASEAN the EU’s third-largest trading partner outside Europe.
The European Union’s investment stock in ASEAN stood at 363.4 billion euros (about $422 billion) in 2024.
Singapore plays an important role in these ties. EU-Singapore trade in goods reached 47.8 billion euros (about $55.4 billion) in 2025. The EU-Singapore Digital Trade Agreement, which entered into force in February 2026, set rules to simplify digital transactions and cross-border trade.
These figures highlight Southeast Asia’s growing importance to European businesses, even in the absence of a comprehensive regional free trade agreement.
Regional agreement and other areas of cooperation
Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said his country would seek progress on an ASEAN-EU free trade agreement during its rotational chairmanship of ASEAN in 2027.
“We understand that this will be difficult. The issue is complex, but we are also somewhat confident about making progress,” Wong said.
The European Union has bilateral free trade agreements with several Southeast Asian countries, while negotiations with others in the region are ongoing. Merz called on the European Commission to coordinate trade ties with Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and India more effectively, saying this would create additional opportunities for European businesses.
Reaching a region-wide agreement could prove difficult because economies differ in their rules, industrial priorities and levels of development.
The European Union and ASEAN are also considering closer cooperation in energy, technology and security. Merz said the EU was ready to support ASEAN’s initiative to connect national electricity grids, a project aimed at strengthening energy links across Southeast Asia.
The two leaders also discussed expanding cooperation in artificial intelligence, sustainable energy, defense and security.
Wong confirmed Singapore’s interest in investing in Germany and the European market as a whole. He said investors, including sovereign wealth funds, remained confident in Europe’s long-term economic prospects.
For the European Union, deepening ties with Asia offers a chance to expand export markets, attract investment and reduce the impact of disruptions to global trade. Whether these plans lead to concrete agreements will depend on the parties’ ability to overcome their economic differences.

OSLO, Norway, Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Europe is facing a historic wave of investments in energy and critical infrastructure. DNB is now launching DNB Fund European Energy Security, a new mutual fund designed to invest in companies helping secure Europe's future energy supply.
"Energy security has become one of Europe's most important strategic priorities. To maintain competitiveness, industrial strength and living standards, Europe needs an energy system that is more resilient, flexible and less dependent on imports," says Mikkel Nyholt, manager of DNB Fund European Energy Security.
The fund invests in companies that provide solutions within energy generation, power grids, energy storage and the protection of critical infrastructure.
Positioned to benefit from major investment needs
Europe faces significant investments in its energy systems over the coming decades. Increased electrification, growing power demand and the need for greater energy independence are driving demand for new infrastructure and technology.
"We are not investing in politics. We are investing in the companies that can win contracts as Europe upgrades and modernises its energy system. This is where we see significant potential for long-term value creation," says Nyholt.
Investing across the entire energy value chain
The fund targets companies operating in four key areas:
- Secure energy supply – power generation, renewable energy, nuclear power and alternative gas suppliers.
- Resilient energy systems – power grids, cables and transformers.
- Flexible energy solutions – energy storage and backup power.
- Protection of infrastructure – cybersecurity and monitoring solutions.
"Energy security is about much more than producing electricity. Energy must also be transmitted, stored and protected. That is why we take a broad approach, investing in companies that are essential across the entire energy value chain," says Nyholt.
A long-term investment theme
According to Nyholt, energy security is a long-term trend that will shape Europe for years to come.
"Europe is undergoing a structural transformation of its energy systems. We believe this will drive substantial investments for decades, and we want to provide our clients with exposure to the companies that can become key beneficiaries of this development," he says.

articles.summary: Reform's third Staffordshire County Council leader in a year steps down  BBCReform UK leader of Staffordshire County Council announces shock resignation | ITV News Central  ITVXNew acting leader appointed at Staffordshire County Council  Lichfield LiveNew Acting Leader for Staffordshire County Council  Staffordshire County CouncilYou can’t get the Staffs: Reform council elects its fourth leader in 17 months  The New European
articles.full_text:
Reform's third council leader in a year steps down
- Published
The Reform UK leader of Staffordshire County Council has announced his decision to step down after seven months in the role.
Martin Murray, who was formally elected in March, confirmed he had resigned as both the authority's leader and as leader of its Reform group on Tuesday, adding it was in the "best interests" of Staffordshire and its residents.
Murray's departure is the latest in a series of leadership changes in Staffordshire since December 2025, following the exits of Ian Cooper and Chris Large.
Deputy leader Hayley Coles had been selected as the party's fourth group leader and would serve as acting leader of the county council, a Reform spokesperson confirmed.
Councillor Coles, who Reform said would be confirmed as leader of the council in December, said: "I am proud to have been trusted to lead our Reform administration and Staffordshire County Council into this new chapter.
"My priority is to drive forward the mandate our residents voted for and deliver the change the county so desperately needs."
Murray would remain as a Reform councillor for Cannock Town, the party confirmed.
Councillor Sean Bagguley, cabinet member for finance and resources, had become acting deputy leader of the council, a spokesperson for the authority added.
In a statement, councillor Murray said it was a "difficult decision" but the interests of Staffordshire and the council "must come first".
He said he was proud of his work to boost investment in Staffordshire and to raise the profile of the county's tourism, leisure and hospitality sectors.
"It has been a privilege to serve the people of Staffordshire and to work alongside dedicated councillors, officers, businesses, community organisations and residents," he said.
"While my time as leader has come to an end, my commitment to Staffordshire and the people of Cannock remains unchanged."
Murray added: "I do wish the council and its new leadership every success in the years ahead."
Murray had previously called for stability at the county council after a period of leadership that first saw Cooper step down over racism allegations linked to social media activity, followed by the departure of Large, who was investigated over racist comments he denied writing.
Cooper, who remained an independent councillor in Tamworth, was subject to an investigation following allegations made against him in December 2025.
In June, the authority confirmed it had not upheld the complaints against the ex-leader, because its investigation found he "was not acting in his capacity as a councillor" at the time.
Councillor Phillip White, leader of the Conservative opposition on the authority, said: "I wish Martin Murray well for the future but it is deeply concerning that Staffordshire County Council - one of the largest local authorities in the country, is now onto its fourth Reform leader in a year and a half."
Newcastle-under-Lyme Labour MP Adam Jogee described the news as "another example of the chaos that dominates county hall".
"Rather than leading with competence, getting a grip and making things work, all we get is chaos and division from those in charge at Staffordshire County Council," he said.
"The people of Newcastle-under-Lyme deserve so much better than this."
BBC Midlands political editor Elizabeth Glinka said Reform's victory in the Staffordshire local elections was "emphathic", having taken 49 out of the 62 seats and "devastating the local conservatives who had run the council for decades".
"With so many new councillors some teething problems were perhaps to be expected, but personnel issues have been a continued distraction for the group," she said.
"Having lost one councillor within weeks of the election over social media posts, this summer another Charlotte Kelly defected to the Conservatives, blaming sexism and bullying within Reform. The party said she had been a source of "ongoing disharmony".
"Fallings out and resignations are hardly unusual in local government, but a fourth group leader in 17 months isn't the advert for strong and stable leadership the party may have hoped for."
The group's first leader Cooper still sits as independent, she said.
"He was expelled from the party for failing to declare social media accounts. One of which showed he was a "top fan" on a white supremacy page on Facebook," Glinka explained.
"His replacement councillor Large, was never actually sworn in as council leader, resigning from the party following alleged racist comments on a social media account bearing his name. He said his account was hacked and continues to sit as an independent."
"Martin Murray's departure makes three. The local party will no doubt be hoping new leader Hayley Coles manages to surpass his seven months in charge."

German semiconductor manufacturer Infineon Technologies is investing US$1.23 billion (€1.1 billion) to expand its chip manufacturing plant in Villach, Austria. Infineon aims to strengthen European chip production as demand for energy-efficient technologies and artificial intelligence infrastructure continues to grow.
The investment will support the development of advanced gallium nitride (GaN) power semiconductor manufacturing capacity at the Infineon’s Austrian site. The facility is also expected to use 300-millimeter wafers to manufacture next-generation power chips. Production is scheduled to begin by the end of 2027 while the investment program is expected to extend through 2034.
Infineon Austrian Chip Manufacturing Facility Expansion
The expansion comes as data centres, particularly those supporting artificial intelligence workloads, require increasingly efficient power conversion and management systems. The pace with which data centres continue to scale-up is also increasing, with expansions such as AirTrunk’s SYD3 hyperscale data centre project in Sydney, Australia progressing wiht development. GaN semiconductors can switch electrical power faster and with lower energy losses than conventional silicon-based technologies in suitable applications. This makes them valuable for high-efficiency power supplies and other demanding electronic systems.
The new manufacturing line is expected to use existing cleanroom capacity at Villach. This will allow Infineon to expand production without relying entirely on the construction of a completely new factory.
The use of 300-millimeter wafers also offers a manufacturing efficiency advantage, as each wafer can yield approximately 2.3 times as many chips as a 200-millimeter wafer. However, this depends on the chip design and production process.
Infineon’s Manufacturing Footprint in Europe
Additionally, the project also builds on Infineon’s established manufacturing footprint in Villach, where the company opened a €1.6 billion power semiconductor factory in 2021. The site serves as a major centre for power electronics research and production. It has expertise spanning silicon, silicon carbide and gallium nitride technologies.
The latest investment also aligns with Infineon’s wider strategy to strengthen its position in power management technologies for AI infrastructure. On October 21, 2026, the company announced a collaboration with NVIDIA on GaN-based power conversion systems for 800-volt direct-current AI data centres. This continues to highlight the growing importance of advanced power electronics as computing infrastructure expands.
The expansion is also expected to reinforce Austria’s role in Europe’s semiconductor supply chain. This is while supporting the development of technologies used in data centres, energy infrastructure, electric mobility, robotics and consumer electronics.
However, further details on the expansion’s construction schedule, additional employment and expected production capacity have not been confirmed yet.
