articles.summary: Kyiv Ballistic Missile Strike Kills 1, Injures 15 in University Area and Multiple Districts  Kyiv PostUkraine war briefing: Russia strikes Kyiv hours before truce begins in war-ravaged city Oleshky  The GuardianExplosions heard in Ukraine's Kyiv, Reuters witness says  ReutersDeadly Russian ballistic missile attack hits Kyiv university, bridge, medical centers  The Kyiv IndependentRussian drones hit two more vessels in Black Sea as Nordic leaders urge Putin...
articles.full_text:
Russian ballistic missiles struck a university campus and surrounding residential areas in Kyiv late Monday, Oct. 26, killing at least one person and injuring over 10 others, most of them students, as emergency crews searched damaged buildings for people feared trapped under rubble.
The strikes hit the grounds of a university near Kyoto Park and Lisova metro station on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, damaging student dormitories, residential buildings, and medical facilities.
Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said nine of the wounded were hospitalized, including three in serious condition.
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that further strikes were possible as Russian Shahed drone attacks continued against the capital and other Ukrainian cities.
“There is extensive damage, and there are also reports that people may be trapped under the rubble,” Zelensky wrote on social media.
The Ukrainian leader stressed that the missiles struck crowded civilian areas where, he said, there were no military facilities nearby.
“Unfortunately, there may be more strikes coming,” Zelensky added.
At 8:30 a.m. on Tuesday, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) reported that the number of casualties had risen to 15.
“Overnight, the enemy attacked the capital with ballistic missiles and [unmanned aerial vehicles] UAVs. As a result of the Russian Federation’s terrorist actions, damage has been recorded in three districts of Kyiv,” the report reads.
Of the 15 casualties, 12 have been hospitalized.
According to the State Emergency Service (DSNS), two fires broke out in non-residential buildings in the Obolonskyi district. Rescuers have extinguished both fires. Two casualties were reported in the district.
In the Holosiivskyi district, the Russian attack damaged transport infrastructure.
University campus and student dormitories damaged
The university affected by the attack was identified as the State University of Trade and Economics (SUTE), located on Kyoto Street in Kyiv’s Desnianskyi district.
The institution, founded in 1946, is one of the capital’s major public universities, with more than 15,000 students across six faculties, according to its official profile.
The university specializes in economics, international trade, finance, law, information technology, and management.
Russia’s ballistic strike landed near a university dormitory, shattering windows and injuring residents, according to Klitschko.
The mayor initially reported that a 20-year-old woman was hospitalized following the strike near the dormitory.
In a subsequent update, Klitschko said most of the 10 people injured in the attack were students living in university accommodation. Nine were taken to hospital.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reported damage to university buildings, dormitories and nearby residential properties.
KMVA also reported damage to a school building in the Desnianskyi district.
A paramedic and an emergency medical technician suffered injuries after their ambulance came under fire in the Desnianskyi district, according to the mayor. Their injuries were not considered critical.
A strike near Lisova metro station also set a private vehicle on fire, while nearby residential infrastructure sustained damage.
In the Dniprovskyi district, a three-story non-residential building was partially destroyed, with emergency workers discovering the body of one person in its basement, according to the State Emergency Service.
The destruction extended across residential, educational and medical facilities in the two districts.
Zelensky urges allies to accelerate air defense deliveries
Zelensky renewed his call for faster deliveries of Western air defense systems and ammunition, warning that delays were leaving Ukrainian cities vulnerable to further Russian missile strikes.
He said Ukraine continued to face a constant threat from ballistic missiles that could strike populated areas with little warning.
Under such circumstances, he argued, “artificial delays in providing air defense to Ukraine help terror.”
The president called for political agreements on defense assistance to be implemented promptly, stressing that Ukraine needed sufficient weapons not only to intercept incoming missiles but also to destroy Russian launchers.
The latest attack came amid an intensified Russian missile and drone campaign against Ukraine, with Kyiv’s residential neighborhoods, transport facilities, and civilian infrastructure repeatedly affected.

articles.title: The City will see through Healey’s borrowing gimmick - The Telegraph
articles.summary: The City will see through Healey’s borrowing gimmick  The TelegraphThe chancellor’s pet PuFins have an important role – but they need more scrutiny | Nils Pratley  The GuardianJohn Healey to give £20bn boost to UK’s business lender and infrastructure bank  Financial TimesUK's Healey to give two state-backed lenders £20 billion capital boost in budget  ReutersChancellor’s £20bn to invest would cost less than £1 billion in headroom: IPPR analysis  ...
articles.full_text:
John Healey told us last month there was nothing progressive about the Government spending £1 in every £10 on debt interest. He went further at the Labour Party conference, calling today’s debt levels an “affront” to his party’s values.
Yet in Wednesday’s Budget, he will announce plans that will increase both.
How does he justify such hypocrisy? Mainly through accounting trickery and a loophole in the Government’s fiscal rules.
Rachel Reeves changed the measure of debt her fiscal rule targets to one based on “public sector net financial liabilities”.
This measure subtracts the value of loans and equity stakes from the state’s liabilities. If the Government borrows to make a loan or buy a stake in a business, the financial asset it acquires initially offsets the new liability under this measure.
But the Government still has to raise the cash for this lending by issuing more government debt. The Debt Management Office must sell gilts to fund it. And the interest payable on these gilts is real, even if the investment looks neutral against the fiscal rule.
So when the Chancellor announces he is giving the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank another £20.4bn of investment capacity over the next five years. This can indeed be accommodated within the fiscal rules. But it is equally true that he will increase government borrowing to fund it.
The Office for Budget Responsibility has warned about this sort of trickery.
They said this rule could mean politicians would be “incentivised to use financing mechanisms such as loans and equity to meet a given policy objective, even if this is not the best value for money mechanism”.
This is what has happened. Determined to avoid headline tax increases yet still wanting to do what all Labour chancellors do: increase public spending, borrow more and hope no one notices.
For someone who has preached fiscal discipline, it’s extraordinary that he thinks he can get away with this.
While £20bn across five years may not be much in the grand scheme, if the full £20.4bn were eventually financed at around 5pc, the gross annual financing cost would be roughly £1bn.
How does that sit with Healey’s values? Or is he happy to cast those aside, as he does with his views on defence spending?
The Chancellor and his allies will no doubt argue that the investments will generate a return. That, even after accounting for financing costs, the Treasury will be net better off. Maybe. But the National Wealth Fund reported a £67.5m pre-tax loss in 2025-26.
That was an improvement on the £152.2m loss it recorded the year before. But if you exclude income from the Sizewell C transaction, the latest loss was £144.4m. This does not mean this additional financing won’t generate a return, but the track record doesn’t guarantee it.
In years to come, the increasing use of these public financial institutions, also known as PuFins, to hide the debt impact of spending will come to resemble the Private Finance Initiative scandals of the last Labour government.
The Chancellor is using a financing structure to make today’s decisions appear painless and leave future governments to manage the consequences. It is as shameless as it is reckless.
Worse still, this isn’t the only borrowing increase the Chancellor is poised to announce.
He is also creating a £1.5bn lending facility for regional mayors, offering cheaper loans to councils that want to build. There is no question that this Government’s answer is more borrowing and more debt.
Healey says fiscal discipline underwrites every promise his Government makes. Yet when faced with demands for extra spending, his instinct is to borrow more rather than find room within the money the Government already spends.
The idea that he couldn’t find £4bn to £5bn a year in genuine savings to fund this sort of investment is ridiculous.
The £20bn will not hit the gilt market on Wednesday. But it will hit it at some point.
Deutsche Bank estimates that the Budget will add almost £10bn a year to the Government’s cash borrowing later this decade, taking its gross financing requirement above £250bn by 2030-31.
More importantly, investors are entitled to ask what happens the next time Healey faces a difficult spending choice and the time after that.
A fiscal rule cannot convince them that borrowing is controlled if every new priority creates another lending facility while decisions on spending and welfare are put off indefinitely.
They will price the Government’s appetite for debt, not just its compliance with a target. That’s how you earn a moron premium. Liz Truss earned hers in a single afternoon. Healey seems content to earn his moron premium one lending facility at a time.

articles.summary: EU energy transition removes firm capacity before grid replacement, raising marginal costs  PravdaReport
articles.full_text:
The European Union's effort to decouple from Russian energy while simultaneously phasing out baseload power sources is creating systemic instability across its economy and social fabric, according to Russian President Vladimir Putin. In an interview with journalist Pavel Zarubin, Putin argued that the haste of the energy transition-specifically the decommissioning of coal plants and nuclear reactors-is compromising the reliability of the energy mix and driving inflation.
Despite political directives from Brussels, the physical flow of Russian energy remains a critical component of European supply. Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) currently accounts for approximately 20% of the European market, with annual procurement volumes ranging between 15 and 17 million tons. A primary driver of this supply is the Yamal LNG project, which directs 85% of its total output toward European markets. Putin noted that while the EU declares a goal of reducing imports, actual procurement volumes remain significant, with some traders increasing purchases ahead of new regulatory deadlines.
The transition toward renewable energy, Putin contends, is being pursued without sufficient regard for economic justification or the physical requirements of a stable grid. By removing firm capacity-provided by coal and nuclear generation-before renewable integration and storage can handle the load, the EU is facing higher marginal costs for power. This increased cost of energy is feeding an inflationary spiral, eroding consumer purchasing power and triggering social unrest. Protests in major cities across France, Belgium, and Spain, which began as sectoral disputes, have evolved into broader demonstrations against current economic policies.
The operational landscape is further complicated by upcoming legislative bans under the RePowerEU directive. The EU intends to prohibit the transshipment of Russian LNG in European ports starting in March 2025, with a total ban on all Russian LNG imports slated for 2027.
These mandates create a legal impasse for major energy firms, including TotalEnergies (France), Naturgy (Spain), and SEFE (Germany). The primary constraint is not just the physical supply, but the validity of long-term contracts. Because the legal mechanisms for redirecting contracted volumes to third countries remain ill-defined, the industry faces significant litigation risk and commercial uncertainty as the window for legal procurement closes.

Donald Trump has declared Brazil’s election was “rigged” after the Left-wing Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was re-elected for a fourth term.
The US president said the vote, which saw Mr Lula beat Flávio Bolsonaro in a surprise turnaround, “looked like another rigged election”.
The 80-year-old, known as Lula, won 51.8 per cent of the vote, compared with Mr Bolsonaro’s 48.2 per cent – a difference of about 4.4 million votes – to secure a non-consecutive fourth term in office.
It was a dramatic comeback after his defeat to Mr Bolsonaro in a first-round vote.
But Mr Bolsonaro, the hard-Right son of Jair Bolsonaro, the former president who also contested Brazil’s 2022 election result, initially refused to concede on Monday. He later said he would lead the opposition to Lula’s government. “To withstand the chaos, I’m going to organise the opposition,” he said.
The 45-year-old had been seeking an annulment because of the Brazilian supreme court’s decision to extend voting for two hours on Sunday. This occurred after Lula said buses had been taken out of service in cities where he drew widespread support.

articles.title: Chinese automakers expand manufacturing in Europe to avoid EU tariffs amid rising domestic competition: Repo.. - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Chinese automakers expand manufacturing in Europe to avoid EU tariffs amid rising domestic competition: Repo..  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
Chinese automotive giants, such as BYD and Geely, are setting up production plants in Europe. This strategic initiative helps them sidestep steep EU import taxes on electric vehicles, significantly lowering costs. By investing more in local manufacturing, they cultivate better connections with European suppliers, boosting operational efficiency.
According to the report, Chinese automakers, including BYD, Chery and Geely, are shifting production closer to European markets amid intense domestic competition and excess manufacturing capacity. Beyond avoiding European Union (EU) tariffs, these companies are leveraging underutilised factories and local partnerships to establish a long-term presence in Europe's automotive industry.
"The expansion marks a new phase in China's global automotive ambitions, testing whether its advantages in cost, scale and electric vehicle technology can be replicated overseas," the report said.
At the same time, it noted, for Hyundai Motor Group, which has spent decades building a European manufacturing network, the transformation brings a "formidable new challenge" as Chinese rivals increasingly compete on its turf.
Hence, local production offers a significant advantage in navigating EU trade restrictions, it noted.
Chinese-made battery electric vehicles (EVs) are subject to a standard 10 per cent import duty in the European Union (EU), along with additional countervailing tariffs ranging from 7.8 per cent to 35.3 per cent, depending on the manufacturer.
BYD faces an additional tariff of 17 per cent, while Geely and SAIC Motor face levies of 18.8 per cent and 35.3 per cent, respectively.
Thus, setting up manufacturing facilities within the EU would enable Chinese automakers to avoid these additional import tariffs, lower shipping costs and strengthen ties with local suppliers.
Notably, other Chinese manufacturers are pursuing similar strategies. SAIC Motor, which sells vehicles primarily under its MG brand, has explored plans for a European production facility as it seeks to reduce reliance on imports from China, the report said.
Additionally, "Chinese automakers are increasingly forming alliances with established manufacturers that are struggling with sluggish demand, costly electrification investments and underused production capacity."
It should also be noted that Chinese brands' European sales jumped 90.6 per cent year-on-year to 531,862 vehicles in the first half of 2026, The Korea Herald reported, citing market research firm MarkLines.
"Chinese manufacturers are expanding beyond battery-electric vehicles into plug-in hybrids and conventional hybrids," it noted.
While this shift may help the struggling European factories stay open, it also raises questions about the region's growing reliance on China.

articles.summary: ECB Meeting: Five key questions on rates, inflation and Lagarde's exit  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The ECB faces a challenging policy environment, with oil prices remaining above $100 a barrel and inflation risks elevated even as tighter financial conditions threaten to weigh on economic growth. Political instability in France and rising government borrowing costs have added to uncertainty surrounding the euro zone economy, the report stated.
Also Read |Global Market: China's yuan hits four-year high as dollar weakens ahead of policy meetings
ECB expected to keep rates unchanged
Economists polled by Reuters expect the central bank to raise rates by 25 basis points in December, reflecting concerns that inflation could remain elevated if energy costs continue to rise.
Eurozone inflation reached 3.8% in September, well above the ECB's 2% target. At the same time, rising government bond yields are tightening financial conditions and could constrain economic activity, complicating the central bank's efforts to balance price stability with growth.
Also Read |Global Market: South Korean shares fall over 1% as AI trade concerns weigh; won strengthens
Energy prices keep inflation risks elevated
The ECB is likely to remain alert to the possibility that higher energy costs could spread to other goods and services, eventually pushing up wages and broader inflation.
However, recent inflation data suggest that these second-round effects remain relatively contained. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, edged up to 2.5% in September from 2.4% previously, indicating that higher energy costs have yet to trigger a more widespread acceleration in prices.
The report stated that comments from ECB officials, including Chief Economist Philip Lane, suggest policymakers are not yet overly concerned about an energy-driven inflation spiral.
Nevertheless, oil prices have risen sharply this year, while a survey released on Friday showed that euro zone consumers increased their inflation expectations for the next 12 months in September.
Markets are pricing in at least two additional rate increases by mid-2027. Further escalation of the Iran war or renewed pressure on energy prices could strengthen the case for additional tightening, even next year.
French bond selloff adds to ECB's challenges
The deterioration in France's public finances and political stability presents another challenge for the ECB as it prepares for its policy meeting.
French 10-year government bond yields have climbed above 5%, reaching their highest levels in 24 years, while political tensions and protests have complicated the government's efforts to address the country's fragile fiscal position.
The premium investors demand to hold French 10-year bonds over German government debt has widened to 167 basis points, compared with 92 basis points at the ECB's previous meeting.
The widening spread reflects growing investor concerns about France's fiscal outlook and the risk that political uncertainty could undermine efforts to control public debt.
However, the ECB is not expected to intervene immediately through its Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which allows it to purchase government bonds to counter unwarranted and disorderly tightening in financing conditions across euro zone member states.
ECB President Christine Lagarde has argued that France must address its debt problems through fiscal consolidation.
The central bank could, however, reconsider the pace of monetary tightening if financial instability in France threatens to significantly weaken economic growth. The report by Reuters stated that the ECB could also use its bond-buying mechanism to prevent a French crisis from spreading to other euro zone economies with stronger public finances, according to the report.
Lagarde's succession emerges as another focus
Investors are also likely to watch for developments concerning Lagarde's future and the succession process at the ECB.
Lagarde could be appointed as the next chair of the World Economic Forum as early as November, potentially bringing forward discussions about who might succeed her as ECB president.
Former central bank governors Klaas Knot of the Netherlands and Pablo Hernandez de Cos of Spain are considered leading candidates for the position.
Her departure would come amid broader changes to the ECB's leadership. The resignation of Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel has opened another vacancy, while Chief Economist Philip Lane is scheduled to step down in May.
Lagarde's current term is due to end in October next year. An earlier departure could allow European leaders to appoint a successor before France's spring presidential election, reducing the risk that domestic political developments could complicate the selection process.
A possible snap election in Spain could also influence the political dynamics surrounding the appointment.
Policy uncertainty likely to persist
The ECB's October meeting comes at a time when policymakers must navigate competing risks from persistent inflation, higher borrowing costs, geopolitical uncertainty and political instability in a major euro zone economy.
Although a pause in interest rates is widely anticipated, investors will scrutinise the central bank's assessment of energy prices, underlying inflation and financial conditions for clues about its next move.
The immediate decision may be straightforward, but the outlook for monetary policy remains uncertain, with the trajectory of the Iran war, oil prices and France's fiscal situation likely to shape the ECB's decisions in the coming months, according to the report.

articles.title: India-EU Free Trade Agreement Raises Trade and Logistics Hopes, Says Rotterdam Port Chief - Bold News
articles.summary: India-EU Free Trade Agreement Raises Trade and Logistics Hopes, Says Rotterdam Port Chief  Bold News

European logistics leaders expect stronger commercial links with India as both sides prepare for the next stage of their trade pact, with smoother cargo movement and market access emerging as key priorities.
ROTTERDAM, October 25: The proposed India-European Union free trade agreement has generated strong expectations among European trade and logistics leaders, with the head of the Port of Rotterdam expressing confidence that closer commercial ties could create new opportunities for businesses on both sides.
Boudewijn Siemons, chief executive officer of the Port of Rotterdam, said Europe was looking forward to expanding business with India and described the potential of the trade agreement as substantial.
His remarks came during a visit by Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal to the Dutch port on Sunday. Discussions included the importance of cooperation between ports and countries to facilitate the movement of goods through international supply chains.
Siemons said improving the flow of goods between India and Europe would be an area of continued work, highlighting the connection between trade policy and logistics infrastructure.
Negotiations for the India-EU free trade agreement were announced as concluded in January 2026. The agreement was expected to be signed by the end of the year, with implementation potentially beginning in 2027, according to a report by The Economic Times citing PTI. 
The anticipated agreement has attracted attention because India and the European Union represent substantial markets with diverse manufacturing, services and consumer industries. However, the eventual commercial benefits will depend on the agreement’s final provisions, implementation arrangements and the ability of companies to use any new market-access opportunities.
Rotterdam’s Strategic Role in India-Europe Trade
The Port of Rotterdam is one of Europe’s major maritime gateways, connecting international shipping routes with industrial centres and consumer markets across the continent.
Its infrastructure supports the movement of containers, energy products, chemicals, raw materials and other cargo. The port is linked to inland transportation networks that allow goods to move onward by rail, road and waterways.
For Indian exporters, access to efficient logistics networks can be as important as tariff reductions. A shipment must move through ports, customs procedures, storage facilities and inland distribution systems before reaching its final customer.
Delays at any stage can increase costs, complicate delivery schedules and reduce the competitiveness of products in overseas markets.
Greater cooperation between Indian and European ports could help businesses coordinate shipping schedules, improve cargo handling and identify bottlenecks in transportation networks.
The benefits would not be limited to large exporters. Smaller manufacturers and trading companies could also gain if improved logistics made overseas shipments more predictable and reduced the cost of moving goods.
For European importers, more efficient connections with India could support sourcing from a wider range of suppliers and provide additional options for industrial inputs and finished products.
Nevertheless, the impact would vary by commodity, route, shipment size and the availability of suitable transport services.
What the Trade Agreement Could Mean for Businesses
A free trade agreement generally seeks to reduce barriers to commerce between participating economies. Depending on its terms, it can address customs duties, market access, services, investment, regulatory cooperation and other issues affecting cross-border business.
For India and the European Union, the agreement could create opportunities for companies seeking to expand trade in both directions.
Indian exporters in sectors such as textiles, engineering goods, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, processed products and selected consumer industries could examine opportunities to strengthen their presence in European markets.
European businesses, meanwhile, could seek to increase sales of industrial machinery, specialised equipment, technology and other products in India.
The precise benefits for individual industries will depend on the final tariff schedules, rules of origin, standards and other commitments included in the agreement.
Tariff reductions can improve price competitiveness, but they do not guarantee higher sales. Exporters must also satisfy product requirements, maintain consistent quality, meet delivery deadlines and establish reliable distribution channels.
Companies entering a new market may need to invest in certification, packaging, after-sales service, local partnerships and compliance procedures.
For smaller firms, these requirements can be difficult to manage without specialist advice or adequate working capital. Trade facilitation measures and accessible information about the agreement will therefore be important in helping businesses take advantage of any new opportunities.
Market Access and Regulatory Requirements
The European Union is a large and diverse market, but access requires exporters to comply with applicable product and regulatory requirements.
Depending on the product, businesses may need to meet standards covering safety, labelling, technical specifications, environmental performance and documentation.
For manufacturers, the ability to demonstrate compliance can influence whether a product is accepted by an importer or distributor.
A trade agreement may reduce certain barriers, but it does not automatically remove every regulatory obligation. Companies will need to understand which requirements apply to their products and how the agreement changes existing procedures.
Rules of origin are another important consideration. These determine whether a product qualifies for preferential tariff treatment under a trade agreement.
Exporters may need to provide documentation showing where goods were produced or how much processing took place in a participating country. Businesses that rely on imported components will need to assess whether their products satisfy the relevant criteria.
Clear guidance on these provisions could help smaller firms avoid mistakes and calculate the actual cost of exporting.
The agreement’s practical value will therefore depend not only on negotiated concessions but also on how easily businesses can understand and use them.
Opportunities for Indian Manufacturing and Smaller Exporters
India’s manufacturing sector includes businesses of different sizes, ranging from large industrial groups to smaller suppliers producing specialised components and finished goods.
Improved access to European customers could encourage some Indian firms to increase production, invest in machinery or seek partnerships with overseas distributors.
Small manufacturers supplying larger exporters may also benefit indirectly if stronger international demand leads to additional orders throughout the supply chain.
For example, a company exporting engineering products may depend on smaller firms for metal components, packaging, tooling or maintenance services. Growth in the final exporter’s business can create opportunities for those suppliers.
However, the relationship between trade access and industrial expansion is not automatic. Businesses must have the capacity to meet larger orders without compromising quality or delivery schedules.
They may also need access to finance to purchase raw materials, upgrade production facilities or carry additional inventory while waiting for payment from overseas customers.
Export diversification can help businesses reduce dependence on a limited number of markets, but entering Europe requires careful assessment of customer preferences, pricing and competition.
Support for export documentation, quality certification, market research and logistics could help smaller enterprises prepare for greater international engagement.
Logistics Efficiency Could Shape the Benefits
Siemons’ comments highlighted the importance of ensuring that goods can move efficiently between India and Europe.
Shipping costs, transit times and the reliability of freight services can influence the final price paid by an importer. Even when customs duties are reduced, inefficient logistics may limit the savings available to exporters and buyers.
Ports play a central role in managing cargo transfers between ships and inland transport systems. Efficient handling, predictable processing and reliable connections can reduce delays and help businesses manage inventory.
International supply chains also require coordination among shipping companies, freight forwarders, customs authorities, warehouses and transport operators.
Improved information sharing can help businesses plan shipments and respond to disruptions. Digital documentation and better tracking systems may also reduce administrative burdens, although their effectiveness depends on the systems used by the different participants.
For India-Europe commerce, transport planning must take account of shipping routes, port capacity, cargo types and the onward movement of goods to their final destinations.
The Rotterdam port chief’s emphasis on cooperation between ports and countries reflects the need to connect trade policy with practical arrangements for moving goods.
Investment and Commercial Partnerships

Indian firms may explore opportunities to establish distribution arrangements, service networks or other commercial links in Europe. European companies may assess opportunities to expand their presence in India or develop closer relationships with Indian suppliers.

articles.summary: UK spending on ‘fairytale’ carbon capture tech is a national embarrassment, chancellor told  The GuardianExclusive: Chancellor warned not to axe North Sea energy project to fund defence in carbon capture 'betrayal'  The ScotsmanWill the UK Axe Carbon Capture Funding in the 2026 Budget?  Energy Digital MagazineEnergy minister outlines carbon capture and the renewal of British industry  Open Access GovernmentOther countries will gladly take CCS capital, skil...
articles.full_text:
Campaigners are calling on the chancellor to cut the government’s £24bn spending plans for “fairytale” carbon capture technologies in favour of funding green schemes that can reliably cut emissions and lower energy bills.
The environmentalist Chris Packham is leading an 11th-hour appeal for the Treasury to use this week’s budget to scale back the government’s “exorbitantly expensive” support for carbon capture, which is now more than the planned spending for the US, the EU, Norway and Japan combined.
He said it was a “national embarrassment” that the government had earmarked £24bn to support a series of carbon capture and storage (CCS) projects developed by big oil companies, including BP and the Norwegian state oil company Equinor, and urged ministers to “put things right”.
“CCS is a tech fairytale,” the naturalist and broadcaster said. “It should be a national embarrassment that the UK is pumping more taxpayer money into it than any other country in the world. This budget is a chance to put things right.”
The intervention comes as the government reportedly plans to reduce the grants available to households hoping to swap their gas boiler for an electric heat pump. This shift is considered crucial to cutting the carbon emitted when heating buildings, which makes up around a fifth of the UK’s total greenhouse gas emissions.
Packham called on the government to safeguard funding promises “that empower households to lower bills” rather than “bankrolling exorbitantly expensive projects with ludicrously uncertain results”.
The leaders of many economies have backed carbon capture technology designed to trap the emissions from fossil fuel infrastructure before they are released into the atmosphere. Proponents believe that piping carbon dioxide into underground storage could provide a permanent climate solution for industries that are unable to replace fossil fuels with cleaner alternatives.
Although there are instances where the technology has worked successfully, many high-cost projects have struggled to progress and there are many examples where carbon savings have proved to be far less than expected. Green groups fear the technology has been promoted by fossil fuel companies to prolong the use of fossil fuels.
Packham said a failure to rein in the planned CCS spending “would be yet another strong signal that this government is putting big oil above people and the planet”.
Aled Dilwyn Fisher, a senior researcher at Oil Change International, said: “It’s worrying that spending on climate is being cut in favour of defence, but cutting support for proven climate solutions while continuing to bankroll unreliable carbon capture projects would add insult to injury.
“This budget should be an opportunity to put public money where it can make a real difference to the climate and help cut people’s energy bills, rather than continuing to gamble billions on the fossil fuel industry’s latest expansion plan.”
Work on the UK’s first CCS projects has begun at the East Coast Cluster near Teesside and Humberside, in north-east England, and at the HyNet Cluster near Merseyside and north Wales, in north-west England.
The second phase of the government’s CCS support plan includes £200m to support the Acorn project in Aberdeenshire, alongside £80m from the Scottish government.
Rosie Hampton, a campaigner at Friends of the Earth Scotland, said over the summer that the government’s climate response was being built on “fantasy plans about turning the North Sea into Europe’s carbon dumping ground” while politicians should be focused on “climate solutions that will improve people’s lives, such as warm homes, better public transport and decent green jobs”.
Martin McCluskey, the parliamentary undersecretary at the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, told an industry event this month that the government remained committed to carbon capture but fiscal pressures may require decisions on the pace of the industry’s development.
The Carbon Capture and Storage Association (CCSA) said the UK’s first projects had already awarded more than £4bn in supply-chain contracts, which could support about 350 UK companies and 5,500 construction jobs.
“Pulling back now would undermine investor confidence, risk leaving infrastructure underused and deepen industrial decline,” said Mark Sommerfeld, the CCSA’s UK director.
“This budget must honour existing commitments, turning today’s progress into lasting growth, energy security and reindustrialisation,” he said.
The government has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Von der Leyen’s Canada ‘associate membership’ spurs battle of words with EU capitals - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Von der Leyen’s Canada ‘associate membership’ spurs battle of words with EU capitals  Euronews.comIt’s hard breaking up with Washington: Why Canada’s European defense turn has limits  POLITICO.euCanada's new relationship with EU will be 'closer to membership' than ever, senior officials say  CBCPresident Costa travels to Montreal for the EU-Canada Summit  Council, European UnionCarney moves to remake Canada alliances as US ties strained  AFP.com
articles.full_text:
Germany, Italy, France and Greece objected to a draft EU-Canada declaration that cites von der Leyen’s ‘associate membership’ offer, as the member states fear legal uncertainty and a precedent for other third countries ahead of the Montreal summit on Thursday and Friday.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made a bombshell offer to Canada: to become the first EU “associate member”. Now the term is proving hard to swallow for several member states, including her own Germany.
Ahead of the EU-Canada summit, meant to chart what many see as the closest partnership between the bloc and a non-member country, European capitals led by Berlin have pushed back against a term that has yet to be clearly defined, five EU diplomats told Euronews.
“The main concern is that this is unknown terminology, it might bring up legal uncertainty and expectations from other third countries,” one of the diplomats said. “This was not communicated previously from the Commission. We don’t know what we are talking about.”
Last week, a revised draft of the joint declaration explicitly mentioned the notion, vowing regular exchanges with Canadian authorities on major policy and regulatory initiatives and to define the full scope of the partnership at the 2027 summit.
Naming the term outright in what would be the first EU official document of major political significance to include it has drawn strong pushback from Germany, Italy and Greece, and scepticism from other countries, including France.
A new draft circulated on Monday evening added wording that distanced member states from the concept, specifying that it was “put forward by the European Commission”.
The text was due to be adopted on Tuesday through the so-called silent procedure, under which a document passes unless a member state objects. Germany, Italy, France and Greece all raised objections before the deadline.
The office of European Council President António Costa is now expected to circulate a new version, with another round of talks at ambassador level on Wednesday, before the summit opens in Montreal on Thursday.
Von der Leyen floated the idea of offering associate membership to Canada in her annual State of the Union speech to the European Parliament in September, with Prime Minister Mark Carney as guest of honour.
The idea had been put to the Canadians before, but it was never discussed with member states or within the Commission, catching capitals including Paris and Berlin off guard.
Even Carney did not seem fully sold on the nomenclature, preferring to call it an “alliance of the future”. “What matters is the substance,” he said when asked whether he was comfortable with the term.
With governments now finalising the joint declaration, to be adopted at the summit on Thursday and Friday, that initial lack of consultation is coming back to haunt the bid.
For Berlin, the main issue is that member states should first define what the cooperation package contains, and only then agree the terms for the declaration, not the other way around.
There is broad consensus on seeking closer cooperation with Canada in areas such as defence, critical raw materials, energy, trade and border security. It is the associate membership label that has drawn scrutiny.
Others took aim at its legal implications, arguing these must be carefully studied before the term enters a political declaration.
“It does not mean anything, it is not in the treaties,” a second EU diplomat said, adding that “we want to find a way to make the concept work.”
Von der Leyen is not new to launching new ideas and forging ahead with initiatives without consulting with the member states. In 2023, she announced a migration deal with Tunisia and was criticised for lacking a formal mandate to do so.
“In the case of Tunisia, member states fully agreed with the objective of reducing arrivals, but they had to say that they did not 100% agree with the way it was done. It is a bit the same case here,” a third diplomat told Euronews.
For this diplomat, the EU should not view the label as merely institutional, but as a way of packaging what would otherwise inevitably look like a sector-by-sector technical exercise in bringing Canada closer to the bloc.
For von der Leyen’s critics, she has a habit of making grand announcements before figuring out the implications. For her supporters, her strength is staying ahead of the curve, setting out a political vision and letting the bureaucratic machinery do the rest.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was the first to propose associate membership, but pitched it as a way to anchor Ukraine to the EU, with security guarantees, as Kyiv progressed through the accession process.
Applying it to Canada carries a very different connotation: it would offer a blueprint for the closest possible partnership with a non-European country that could never join the bloc.
“A lot of other countries want to come closer to the EU, but we don’t know what to offer them. Whatever deal we reach with Canada might be an important motivator for others,” an EU official told Euronews.

articles.summary: ‘No one saves the planet if it hits their pocket’: UK heat pump installers fear planned subsidy cuts  The GuardianI’m Britain’s biggest energy boss – scrapping help for heat pumps is a gift to Russia  The i PaperFury as Labour's £2bn Budget fund grab 'will put thousands of jobs at risk overnight'  AOL.co.ukThe Cut: Big decisions are imminent  The Eco Experts2023 increase to heat pump grant raised installations by 24% a month, study finds  The Lon...
articles.full_text:
When Bill Tuck first started installing air source heat pumps six years ago, other heating engineers were skeptical about whether the green technology would take off. “Now, the conversation is completely different,” he said.
“I’m getting approached by them saying: ‘Mrs Jones, my customer for 15 years, she’s enquiring about a heat pump. What can you tell me?’ The whole narrative has changed.”
But despite a surge in interest in cheap and sustainable ways to warm homes, the government is understood to be slashing the amount of money available to subsidise heat pumps as it looks for ways to cut spending in Wednesday’s budget.
Businesses that install the renewable systems are fearing the worst. “It’s going to damage us as a company,” said Tuck, the operations director at Sustain Homes in Watford. About 75% of his customers pay for their pump using the government subsidies. “It’s the foundation of the business. If that’s to go, it’s extremely damaging.
“Of course, we will do what it takes to keep everybody’s jobs going and the business afloat. But it’s a tough one – I don’t know how we will do that.”
The boiler upgrade scheme (BUS) was introduced in 2022 to help people decarbonise their homes and businesses. It provides upfront grants worth up to £9,000 to help property owners replace fossil fuel and direct electric heating systems with low-carbon alternatives such as heat pumps and biomass boilers.
Heat in buildings is responsible for approximately nearly a fifth of the UK’s greenhouse gas emissions, the latest government data shows. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has described the 2020s as a “critical decade for decarbonising heat”, but now appears to be putting the cost of decarbonising on to the consumer. The UK lags far behind other European countries with heat pump installation; Norway, the global leader, has 632 installed for every 1,000 households, while the UK has a paltry 3.5.
Jim Lacey, who has been installing renewables with his business JLN Plumbing & Heating for 20 years, said: “No one’s going to save the planet if it really hits their pocket.”
“We can go in [to homes] now and go: ‘It’s a few hundred pound more than having a normal boiler, but you save so much on your energy usage.’ That whole argument’s gone.”
Adam Killa, the founder of Ask Renewables in Burscough, Lancashire, saw what happens when subsidies are removed after the 2022 closure of the Renewable Heat Incentive, a scheme that paid households for generating clean heat.
“As soon as that stopped, we went from doing six, seven, eight [installs] a week down to zero. The customers say: ‘Well, I know they’re good, but 15 grand – I can buy a new boiler for three grand. What’s the point?’
While the government continues its drive to increase numbers of young people earning while learning, heat pump installers say cuts to the subsidy will put their apprentices – and the future of the industry – are at risk.
“Unless we start bringing the young generation through, we’re going to have a huge lack of installers, repair engineers, and more importantly, heat pumps as well,” said Tuck.
A nascent industry, installers fear manufacturers will go under too. According to the Heat Pump Association, about a third of heat pumps sold in the UK in 2024 were produced domestically.
“This isn’t just down to us fitting the heat pumps, it’s the people delivering them, it’s the people manufacturing them, it’s all the associated trades that go with it that make the little bits, the little bobs, everything,” said Lacey. “There’s so many knock-on effects”
James Meadway, an economist and co-director of the green thinktank Verdant, said removing money from green jobs and manufacturing would damage Andy Burnham’s mission to effectively reindustrialise Britain. “It’s at a point where his blank spot on climate is working hard against other things he wants to do,” he said.
Lacey said that, while he had not thought the grant would last for ever, he had expected business and consumers to be weaned off gradually as the technology became more widespread and production costs fell. “But to suddenly axe some off the BUS grant or get rid of it completely is just catastrophic for all the work that we’ve put in so far,” he said.
A government spokesperson said: “We do not comment on budget speculation.
“We remain committed to bringing down bills for families now, while investing in the clean, homegrown energy and warmer homes that will protect households from volatile fossil fuel prices for good.”
